This study examines the generalization error of two-layer neural networks when solving high-dimensional Schr\"odinger eigenvalue problems. This result stems from the observation that the expected generalization error is bounded by the square root of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) variance, which itself is upper-bounded by a constant dependent on the network's width, architecture, and activation functions. Consequently, as long as the neural network's width remains modest relative to the training data volume, the error approaches a constant limit. This finding elucidates why neural networks often outperform traditional numerical methods in solving high-dimensional Schr\"odinger eigenvalue problems, demonstrating that their superior generalization capabilities arise from the neural tangent kernel mechanism.

Experimental results indicate that incorporating these contextual covariates significantly enhances prediction accuracy compared to models relying solely on latent variables. However, the presence of severe path loss and blockage in millimeter-wave frequencies restricts the reach of these systems. To address this, we introduce a hybrid encoding framework that integrates traditional coding with multicasting-based coding to enhance mmWave multicasting performance. This scheme employs basic coding within line-of-sight (LoS) conditions and multicasting-based coding for non-line-of-sight (NLoS) environments. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves a 100% increase in throughput and an additional 100% in coverage compared to the baseline systems.

Nuclear masses are essential for analyzing nucleosynthesis, particularly regarding the rapid neutron-capture ($r$-process) phenomenon. However, most nuclei of interest lie beyond the limits of current experimental capabilities. The proliferation of diverse data sources, formats, and sources has created significant challenges for researchers and practitioners in the field of data analytics. To address this, we introduce the H4M dataset, specifically tailored for socioeconomic analysis. This new resource comprises four distinct collections—H4M-P (Poisson), H4M-I (Image), H4M-T (Text), and H4M-V (Vector)—each containing unique, multi-source, and multi-modal data. These collections are heterogeneous, as they consist of heterogeneous types, such as time series, images, text, and vectors, and are derived from various sources, including government and non-government entities, as well as open and closed-access data. To facilitate comprehensive analysis, we have developed a specialized database, the H4M-DB, capable of storing and processing these varied datasets. This tool enables users to perform diverse socioeconomic analyses, such as anomaly detection, forecasting, and classification, on the integrated H4M-DB. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dataset designed specifically for heterogeneous data analytics within the socioeconomic domain.

This study introduces a visual design-driven method for navigating large-scale datasets. Specifically, it converts the characteristics of complex data into corresponding visualization elements. By leveraging human perceptual capabilities, the approach enables design-guided examination of results. We outline the core design principles and present two distinct algorithms that convert data characteristics into visual representations. Additionally, we describe a design-driven system capable of dynamically generating interactive visualizations to explore a dataset's inherent features. Experimental results demonstrate the method's ability to reveal significant insights within large data collections.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant force in machine learning, particularly within node classification tasks. However, training GNNs from scratch is often prohibitively expensive, especially when dealing with limited data or scenarios where the test distribution diverges from the training data. This paper investigates how transfer learning can address these challenges. We introduce a straightforward yet potent transfer learning framework for GNNs that leverages knowledge from an unlabeled source domain to enhance performance. We evaluate our method using two node classification benchmarks: Cora and Facebook Nodes. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts accuracy across both datasets, establishing itself as a highly effective and computationally efficient solution.

The growing volume of data in recommender systems has intensified the need for efficient computational methods. This study introduces a novel dual feature allocation (DAF) model, which simultaneously incorporates user-item ratings along user and item descriptive data to generate precise recommendations. By creating a probabilistic framework that regulates the collaboration strength between user and item features and establishes independent distributions for ratings and observed observations, the system achieves effective performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the recommended system generates superior outputs compared to existing methods.

This work introduces a streamlined proof technique for the set separation problem, recently established by Braverman et al. (FOCS 2021) and recognized as the most recent advancement in this domain. In doing so, they achieve the most compact bit requirements for $s-t$ reachability bitpackets known to date. Moreover, they present the first bitpackets that enable the construction of a set separation in sublinear time.

The spin susceptibility of the Heisenberg paramagnetic state, derived from the one-magnon-reduction formula, is established to be proportional to the inverse square of the wave vector, $k^{-2}$. This is demonstrated to be a direct consequence of the Goldstone theorem and the associated Dirac delta function residing at the zero-magnon energy. Furthermore, this vector's dependence is shown to be a universal feature for all Heisenberg magnets. Additionally, this non-analytic behavior is found to influence the critical behavior of the magnetic phase transition in low-dimensional systems, specifically those with dimensions $d \leq 3$.

Integrated photonic platforms offer significant potential for trapping atom-based quantum interfaces, which serve as a foundational component for various photonic quantum computing and communication systems. In this work, we present a novel architecture featuring three gratings fabricated directly on an on-chip waveguide. This setup allows for the trapping of a single atom via near-field interactions, while two additional gratings in the far-field enable the reading and manipulation of the atom's quantum state. This all-in-one design is fabricated using an established, large-scale production process. We successfully achieved high single-atom trapping efficiency and demonstrated the coherent control and detection of the atom via Rydberg-mediated quantum state transitions. This suggests the feasibility of deploying this quantum interface within larger, scalable photonic quantum computing architectures.

This study examines the impact of electron interactions on the Hall and nonlinear Hall conductances within the Abelian $p + ip$ superconductor, utilizing the self-consistent $t$-matrix approach to incorporate both interactions and disorder. Our findings demonstrate that the Abelian $p + ip$ superconductor retains its characteristic conductance values despite the presence of electron interactions. A key challenge in this approach is the need to estimate patient-specific model parameters, which are typically unmeasured. Consequently, the paper introduces a novel optimization technique that integrates system identification with model predictive control, enabling the simultaneous determination of patient respiratory dynamics and the optimal control solution. This combined framework ensures accurate parameter learning alongside high-performance control outcomes.

This study introduces a new approach for optimizing mirror arrangements in X-ray telescopes, aiming to maximize field of view (FOV) while maintaining high image quality. We define a "twisted" configuration, where components are stacked with a rotation relative to one another, as an extension of nested configurations. By analyzing FOV and image quality metrics, we demonstrate that this design enables FOVs exceeding 10 degrees while preserving focal ratios ($f$-numbers) below 2. We evaluate FOVs using the average of the squared FOV radii ($\langle r^2 \rangle$) and image quality via the normalized Strehl ratio, calculated as the ratio of the Fourier transform of the point spread function to the diffraction limit. Our results confirm that four-mirror nested configurations achieve a $\langle r^2 \rangle$ FOV of 12.5 degrees with a normalized Strehl ratio of 0.5. We further explore the impact of segmentation on performance using these same metrics.

Twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) serves as a prominent model for investigating flat-band systems. In this work, we examine TBG under an external magnetic field, utilizing the magnetic Bloch theorem to construct a magnetic version of the tight-binding model. This formulation reveals that a magnetic flux of $2\pi$ restores the appearance of flat bands. Furthermore, the flat bands exhibit Chern numbers of $\pm 1$ under this flux. The paper also includes a visual representation of the corresponding wavefunctions.

This paper introduces a method for encoding secret binary messages within generated text by training a Long Short-Term Memory network. The study examines two distinct modeling strategies: one utilizing character sequences and another using byte sequences. Experimental results indicate that the byte-based model outperforms the character-based alternative in terms of both message concealment accuracy and overall generation quality. Furthermore, comparisons with a character encoding-based model reveal that employing fixed-character tokens yields a marginal performance gain.

Unit commitment (UC) is a critical process in power systems that determines the optimal scheduling of power plant output and commitment status over a specified time frame. Solving UC involves addressing a complex mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) challenge, which is typically linearized into a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem for resolution using standard solvers. However, these conventional approaches often struggle with scalability and solution speed when dealing with large-scale systems. To address these limitations, this study introduces a machine learning (MLP)-based constraint examination method for UC. By training an MLP model on historical data to learn the relationship between plant operating states and the cost of constraint violations, the model can rapidly predict feasibility. This innovative approach allows for the integration of detailed physical constraints and nonconvex loss equations into UC frameworks without compromising the computational efficiency of MILP solvers. Experimental results on both single and multi-terminal networks demonstrate the method's effectiveness in facilitating the consideration of realistic constraints within the UC optimization process.

We report on the synthesis and characterization of single crystals of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, a material known as a "Kitaev substance." Our analysis confirms that the crystal structure features a buckled triangular lattice with a symmetry consistent with space group $P2_1ab$. Using X-ray diffraction, we tracked structural changes as pressure was applied, revealing a first-order phase transition to an orthorhombic symmetry ($Pbam$) space group at approximately 11 GPa. This transition involves a significant compression of the buckled layers, which is hypothesized to facilitate the emergence of superconductivity. Additionally, we observed a substantial reduction in magnetic ordering temperature ($T_{\text{N}}$) with increasing pressure, dropping from 25 K to roughly 10 GPa. This behavior is attributed to weakened magnetic exchange interactions caused by the expansion of the intratriangular bond distances.

The synthetic control method is a widely adopted technique for estimating treatment effects in scenarios with a limited number of time series. This paper introduces a unified framework for identifying and inferring treatment effects in synthetic control models, grounded in the nearby causal inference model. We demonstrate that the synthetic control method is a specific instance of the nearby causal inference model and establish that the estimator is asymptotically normal, provided the number of controls increases sufficiently. Furthermore, we establish that the estimator exhibits a minimax rate of convergence. To enhance finite-sample performance, we propose a modified version called the synthetic control with projection method, which incorporates additional theoretical guarantees. We validate the proposed methods through a simulation study and by applying them to the analysis of Iran's nuclear program.

The Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance serves as a metric for assessing structural dissimilarity between graphs, with its computation via optimal transport often formulated as a relaxation on a continuous metric space. Although current algorithms for GW distance are well-suited for centralized environments, they fall short in distributed settings where data resides across multiple parties, as they necessitate the exchange of sensitive information. To address this, we introduce a private variant of the GW distance calculation designed for distributed topological graphs. Our approach combines the differential privacy concept with game theory to enable secure communication while ensuring robust privacy protection. We empirically validate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that the proposed private GW distance remains effective within different privacy regimes.

Although the majority of existing work on Deep Image Tinting concentrates on single-camera scenarios, real-world applications frequently involve multiple cameras. We introduce "Cross-Camera Deep Tinting," an approach designed to transfer colors from one camera to another. Our strategy relies on the observation that images of the same object captured by different cameras under identical lighting conditions will exhibit consistent coloration. We propose two distinct architectures: a naive model that applies a single global color transformation across the entire frame, and an advanced, image-aware model that performs local color matching on specific image regions. Both approaches are trained using a composite loss function combining adversarial loss with a novel loss function based on color distance metrics.

This study explores the generalized $n$-dimensional (ND) Hamiltonian Ermakov system, a framework pivotal to various areas of physics. Our analysis reveals that while the ND system's preservation of symmetry relies on specific constraints involving its dimension, it deviates significantly from the conventional one-dimensional (1D) case. Consequently, unlike the 1D scenario, the ND system does not universally admit an equivalent set of point symmetries that are also coordinate transformations. We identify the precise conditions under which the ND Hamiltonian remains invariant, detailing the specific symmetries and preservation laws for both general and specific cases. Furthermore, we establish that the integration of the full ND system generally necessitates solving only a subset of its equations, specifically an $n$-dimensional harmonic oscillator alongside the corresponding 1D-like Ermakov equation. Finally, we outline the general procedure for deriving conservation laws and explicitly calculate invariants for the most basic forms of this ND system.

To achieve accurate ephemeris prediction, the Unobtainable Transit System (UTS) is a vital component of the Global Positioning System (GPS). While the UTS specification was recently made public, the dataset required to compute the model parameters remains unavailable. Consequently, the entire scientific community must rely on existing implementations hosted within public repositories. This paper introduces a novel approach for estimating the UTS model parameters using a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). By training on the historical data provided in the specification, the model achieves a 99.99% improvement in estimation accuracy compared to prior methods.

Few-shot learning addresses the difficulty of classifying new data with limited samples by leveraging the prior knowledge of existing classes. This paper introduces a new approach that derives prototypes from unlabeled data to facilitate this process. The study first analyzes the prototype distribution across different classes and proposes a new method to determine the optimal number of clusters. Subsequently, it introduces a new metric for measuring the distance between prototypes and query points. Finally, it validates the method on standard few-shot learning benchmarks, demonstrating that the approach surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques.

We establish a fresh version of the Goldstone theorem tailored for persistent non-invertible symmetries, even in the absence of spontaneous symmetry breaking. Building on the concept of a generalized order parameter applicable to fractal topological order, we demonstrate that the correlation of this quantity remains non-zero across all distances when the non-invertible symmetry is preserved. Furthermore, we illustrate that within 1+1 dimensional spin chains, persistent non-invertible symmetries can exist without generating any gap in the spectrum.

A graph is semi-transitive if it lacks transitivity yet satisfies the condition that whenever edges $xy$ and $yz$ exist, the closure $xyz$ is transitively closed. While every semi-transitive undirected graph constitutes a chordal bigraph (or is a chordal bigraph in general), determining whether a given chordal bigraph admits an orientation to become a semi-transitive directed chordal bigraph (or is a bigraph chordal bigraph in general) is NP-complete. This paper establishes that the decision problem concerning the existence of an orientation to become a semi-transitive directed chordal bigraph (or is a bigraph chordal bigraph in general) remains NP-complete when restricted specifically to split chordal bigraphs.

This paper introduces the application of a deep neural network (NN) to distinguish between hadronic $\tau$-lepton decays and jets originating from quarks. The hadronic $\tau$ decay signature is characterized by numerous jets produced from quarks alongside several neutral pions ($\pi^0$) and charged pions ($\pi^\pm$). The methodology described is designed to identify these signatures, specifically targeting the $\tau$-to-two-pion ($2\pi$) and $\tau$-to-four-pion ($4\pi$) decay channels. The identification performance for these channels is evaluated using the hadronic $\tau$-lepton sample derived from the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHL) during 2015 and 2016 proton-proton collision runs at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully identifies hadronic $\tau$-to-$2\pi$ and $4\pi$ decays with an efficiency of 70% and 60%, respectively, while maintaining a rejection rate of 99.9% for jet-like background events.

Neural networks have become indispensable tools for addressing challenges across numerous scientific disciplines, a utility that has been solidified by their exceptional performance on the widely used MNIST benchmark for digit categorization. Despite this success, questions remain regarding their reliability in the context of big data applications. Specifically, it is unclear whether Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) can effectively replace standard networks in classification tasks within large-scale projects like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). This study investigates this issue by comparing BNNs against conventional networks through various experiments, including classification of simulated galaxy images and analysis of real galaxy data from the DES Legacy DR4 dataset. Our findings indicate that while BNNs offer distinct advantages in uncertainty quantification, they exhibit slower training speeds and lower accuracy compared to standard neural networks.

This study introduces a novel type of all-homogeneous fiber structure: a solid-core photonic lattice fiber (PLF). We demonstrate that this design supports two distinct transmission modes: single-mode and multi-modal. In the single-mode configuration, we observe strong intermodal Brillouin scattering (IBS), where energy transfers from the fundamental mode to a first excited mode. Conversely, the multi-modal configuration exhibits a significantly reduced IBS effect. Theoretical analysis reveals that the strong scattering observed in single-mode PLFs stems from the high overlap between the modes' electric fields. This characteristic makes these fibers highly suitable for applications involving multi-wavelength or multi-frequency laser pumping.

We offer a fresh proof of the "fundamental theorem" regarding $\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{n}$ Coxeter groups, initially established by the second author for alternating groups and subsequently extended to the B-type by a collaboration. In contrast to traditional methods, our strategy relies on a "geometric" framework, a concept inspired by the first author's work on alternating groups. This approach reveals a profound link between the Cayley graph of these groups and the $\mathrm{n}$-dimensional hypercube, while simultaneously allowing for a fresh examination of the "Cayley-Color Theorem" in both the alternating and B-type contexts.

This study introduces a tabu-inspired local search algorithm designed to tackle the set-union knapsack problem (S-Union-BCP) and the budget-constrained maximum coverage problem (BMCP). Both problems involve selecting a subset of disjoint item groups to maximize total weight within a specified capacity limit; the S-Union-BCP variant permits sharing of weight across distinct groups, whereas standard BMCP does not. We evaluate our approach on two BMCP test sets and a newly created S-Union-BCP benchmark. Our results demonstrate that the method achieves superior solution quality and execution speed compared to a standard local search implementation.

This study introduces a new churn forecasting approach for gamblers in an online gambling platform by integrating game activity data with deposit and betting transaction records. By applying Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to the chat logs from the platform's live support, we engineered features that quantify player engagement intensity. These NLP-derived metrics were combined with traditional features representing the distribution of deposit and betting activities to model churn. To predict loss, the research evaluates three methods: Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting Machines, and Deep Neural Networks. The results indicate that Gradient Boosting Machines deliver the strongest performance, achieving an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.800, surpassing the previously best result of 0.778. Furthermore, the analysis utilized SHAP (SHAPley Additive exPlanations) to identify the most significant predictors of churn, revealing that churners exhibit a distinct preference for high-intensity gameplay compared to those who remain active.

The ratio of the denominator to numerator in f_g lattice P(x) eliminates the renormalization factor, leaving only a dependence on the soft-collinear gluon transverse momentum relative to the lattice direction. To extract TMDPDFs, this ratio is multiplied by renormalization factors and then convolved with a universal soft function. Finally, to account for lattice artifacts, the results are extrapolated to the continuum limit as the lattice spacing vanishes.

Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions generate ultra-central electromagnetic (EM) fields that are orders of magnitude stronger than typical laboratory conditions, enabling the study of quantum electrodynamics (QED) in extreme environments. This work examines the QED dynamics of EM interactions between low-momentum virtual photons and EM fields within ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Utilizing an impact parameter-dependent photon structure function, we analyze QED effects such as photon-nucleus interactions, specifically focusing on the interplay between virtual photons and nuclear charges. Our analysis reveals that the nuclear form factor significantly influences the kinematic distribution of scattered particles, particularly for transverse momenta below 100 MeV/c. This study provides a theoretical basis for future experimental investigations of QED phenomena in ultra-high-energy nuclear collisions.

This work introduces a context-aware and video-based risk measurement model for cyclists. The proposed framework relies on specific risk descriptors for cyclists, which are determined by analyzing video frames to identify key contextual elements such as the cyclist's speed, the presence of sidewalks, lane markings, and traffic density. By leveraging computer vision techniques to detect and track the cyclist within each frame, the system calculates instantaneous risk based on real-time contextual data. Experimental results indicate that this method achieves a correlation coefficient of 0.85 with human-annotated ground truth, representing a substantial improvement over prior methods.

Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) have emerged as a potent formal method for guaranteeing safety-critical system guarantees within barrier function frameworks. Yet, when integrating CBFs with motion planning algorithms, two significant hurdles remain: first, securing robustness against conflicting safety requirements, and second, ensuring robustness regarding modeling inaccuracies and disturbances. This paper proposes a novel C-based motion planning framework designed to generate robust and secure trajectories for robotics within complex, real-world environments. Our approach employs covering sets to define safety regions and utilizes covering barrier functions to establish secure constraints. Furthermore, covering barriers are transformed into convex quadratic constraints via the S-procedure, ensuring a convex representation of the problem. To achieve this, we introduce a covering motion planning algorithm that generates a secure and robust path by optimizing the parameters of these covering barriers. Numerical simulations and real-world robotic experiments validate the efficacy of our proposed method.

Dilation surfaces, which are complex manifolds equipped with a singular flat metric possessing a special real holomorphic structure, are the focus of Morse-Smale analysis. By examining the dynamics of the real structure, we investigate gradient flows that originate and terminate at singularities. These flows reveal that the moduli space of the surface decomposes into a stratification where each stratum corresponds to a specific flow outcome. A key feature of this analysis involves horizon saddle connections, defined as unique geodesics in the flow limit. In the limit, these form links that bound specific regions of the surface. We demonstrate that these links are geometrically significant: they can be defined as critical elements of a specific functional over configurations of closed curves, which we term "horizon saddle links." This characterization holds for any given flow and provides a bridge to understanding the moduli space, as the horizon links of the critical flows directly determine the strata. Furthermore, we explore the existence of multiple saddle connections within the flow and discuss its implications for the dynamics and geometry of dilation surfaces.

This study investigates the functional brain connectivity of the human mind using a 208-region parcellation derived from resting-state fMRI data. The approach models the brain as a probabilistic graphical network where nodes represent distinct cognitive functions and edges capture the probabilistic dependencies among them. By employing total correlation—a mutual generalization of mutual information—we assess the multivariate independence within the brain's functional connectome. Our analysis reveals that total correlation is significantly higher within intra-hemispheric connections than in inter-hemispheric links, indicating stronger internal coordination within each hemisphere. Furthermore, a pronounced non-linear relationship exists between total correlation and pairwise mutual information, suggesting that the functional connectome exhibits complex, non-linear interactions. These findings offer new perspectives on the structure and dynamics of the brain's functional network.

Gaussian fields are widely utilized as spatial random models across various disciplines. Although marginal distributions are often straightforward, they are rarely sufficient for practical applications. In many cases, valid inference requires conditioning on specific observations, such as those from noisy sensors. This study introduces a general methodology for conditioning Gaussian fields along arbitrary paths, with a particular emphasis on scenarios where data is available only at non-regular locations like rational points. The approach involves constructing the field by conditionally extending a partially observed subfield and defines the resulting conditional measure as the conditionally observed field. We demonstrate that this construction yields a version of the field that is both strongly continuous and conditionally null-complemented with respect to the observed path. Furthermore, we establish that when the field is observed along a sufficiently regular and sufficiently dense path, the resulting measure coincides with the original, unconditioned field in a strong sense.

In recent years, the integration of supervised learning techniques into reinforcement algorithms has significantly boosted sample efficiency. A primary driver for this success is the utilization of prioritized experience replay (ERP), which leverages supervised loss functions to sample training data based on a priority distribution. However, the direct application of standard ERP to policy gradient methods has proven problematic, as the greedy sampling strategy can destabilize policy updates. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a novel algorithm termed Variance-Reduced ERP (VREPO). This approach stabilizes policy gradients by minimizing the variance of the policy network's parameter updates. Unlike traditional ERP schemes that select actions solely based on stored state distributions, our method incorporates action sampling from the current policy using a temperature-controlled distribution. This allows ERP to sample actions proportionate to the agent's evolving policy rather than remaining stuck in historical state distributions. Empirical evaluations across continuous control environments demonstrate that VREPO achieves superior performance compared to both standard ERP variants and other recent ERP approaches.

The study compares two distinct approaches to generating integral representations for inverse matrix functionals: the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization equation. Human motion is a fundamental form of communication, yet accurately forecasting its spatiotemporal dynamics remains a significant technical hurdle. MoDeRNN represents human movement through two complementary modalities: temporal profiles, which track the evolution of motion characteristics over time, and spatial maps, which visualize feature distribution across the ground plane. By leveraging the recurrent capabilities of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, the model learns to forecast the evolution of these aspects. Evaluation on two benchmark datasets demonstrates that MoDeRNN surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in predictive performance. Additionally, qualitative analysis of the generated motion aspects reveals a consistent and comprehensive representation of the motion trajectory, thereby offering a clearer understanding of the underlying dynamics and enhancing interpretability.

This paper introduces a method for belief-propagation list decoding that leverages the special properties of polar codes. A key finding is that the polar dual of a polar subcode is precisely the set of its information bits. This duality allows the decoder to resolve the complex interactions between multiple codeword components, effectively breaking the problem down into several simpler decoding subproblems. When merging images with distinct point spread functions (PSFs), the resulting PSF is not merely a simple combination; it depends on the relative scaling of the sources. This phenomenon is illustrated using Gaussian PSFs, where the resulting function's full width at half maximum (FWHM) is determined by a weighted sum of the individual PSF radii. Specifically, image radii contribute to the merge based on their contrast ratios relative to one another. This relationship is further expressed through the Fourier domain, demonstrating that the merged PSF represents a linear combination of the component PSFs with Fourier-domain coefficients that are themselves Gaussian.

Fracture in crystals is modeled as a sequence of atomic bond breakages, where the energy required to split a crystal along a specific plane is calculated as the average bond strength across that surface. This approach yields accurate predictions for fracture strength in various crystal structures, including diamond, zinc blende, and wurtzite. Fracture strength is highly sensitive to the position of atoms within their potential energy wells; notably, shifting atoms from their relaxed equilibrium state to positions with lower potential energy can significantly enhance this strength. Furthermore, since bond strength correlates with the spacing between atoms, materials featuring stiff bonds and small interatomic distances are expected to exhibit superior fracture resistance.

We present an overview of our recent work on chordal Schram-Loofven evolution (SLE) curves connected to one another and embedded within the unit disk. In our analysis, these curves interact through coordinates of a two-dimensional Coulomb gas, specifically a multivariate random log-gas. Our findings reveal that this coupling generates new conformal invariant distributions for the Gaussian free field (GFF), which are characterized by singularities occurring at the tips of the SLE paths. Furthermore, these conformal structures extend beyond the bounded domain to include configurations involving the full plane and the upper half-plane.

In this work, the authors utilize the maximum principle to derive key $C^k$ norms of the velocity within the periodic solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations. These newly obtained $C^k$ norms serve as essential tools for developing maximum principle-based $C^k$ estimates for the velocity field.

Since the inception of quantum computing, researchers have sought efficient methods to verify the correctness of these processes. While recent advancements have achieved constant-time verification for specific outputs, they often fail to address general cases or come with complex implementation details. This study introduces a straightforward and versatile framework capable of verifying traditional quantum computations in linear time. Our method employs a standard interactive proof system where the verifier's total runtime remains linear with respect to the original circuit depth, representing the most efficient verification approach to date for quantum circuits of this nature.

This paper outlines the design of an integrated IoT blockchain framework aimed at facilitating transparent and secure data management. The proposed system combines blockchain with centralized nodes to overcome the central blockchain's limitations regarding resource-constrained IoT devices, which often lack the necessary processing power. While this hybrid approach leverages the decentralization of blockchain, it still relies on specific points of centralization. Consequently, the authors introduce MedFood, an innovative mediation layer built upon this hybrid structure that utilizes specialized oracles and smart contracts to facilitate seamless communication between IoT devices and the blockchain network. The practicality and efficacy of MedFood are validated through a functional prototype designed to support efficient and secure food supply chain operations.

Cell morphology is a critical factor in cellular function and development, and its ability to change underlies essential processes like mitosis. We introduce a neural field framework that models cellular shape using implicit functions to encode signed distance fields, capable of generating realistic cell forms and their variations. Our approach synthesizes images of diverse orientations for each generated shape and trains a generative model capable of producing pairs consisting of a shape and specific viewpoint. This enables the synthesis of high-quality, realistic datasets for validation. We demonstrate that the parameters of our generative model can directly serve as latent variables for generating distinct variations of a specific cell shape. Additionally, we show that the learned representations effectively approximate complex morphological metrics, such as roundness and elongation, which are crucial for cancer research.

This study introduces a new research domain focused on the specific challenges faced by individuals using assistive technology to consume printed materials. While existing solutions primarily convert hard-copy documents into audio, they frequently fail to convey spatial layout and internal structure. We define this missing capability as "document navigability," representing the capacity to move through a document's layout and structural hierarchy. Our work begins by identifying the core functionalities users need to effectively "navigate" a document, then develops a formal model to guide the construction of robust print-to-multi-modal conversion tools.

We introduce a new pre-training and optimization framework for language tasks that extends the capabilities of the Transformer model. By addressing the limitations of auto-regressive approaches, which are constrained by unidirectional context, we integrate the bidirectional strengths of encoder architectures while retaining auto-regressive advantages. Specifically, we employ attention masks to harness bidirectional information within a generative framework. Additionally, we replace auto-regressive token generation with an auxiliary auxiliary model that ranks permutations based on likelihood. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach surpasses both BERT and GPT, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across numerous benchmarks in linguistic understanding and generation.

Stellar activity can mimic or mask atmospheric signals in exoplanet transit spectroscopy, potentially leading to erroneous conclusions. We investigate the efficacy of high-resolution spectroscopy in addressing this issue, utilizing the PASTEL (Planetary Atmospheric Study with Transiting Exoplanets with Low- and High-Resolution) simulation to model the combined spectral signatures of stellar phenomena and planetary transit. Our analysis indicates that stellar activity significantly impacts low-resolution transmission spectra, specifically at wavelengths around 760 nm caused by Earth's O2, and 720 nm caused by its H2O. Conversely, we demonstrate that high-resolution spectroscopy can effectively separate these overlapping spectral features from both the star and the planet. This finding suggests that utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy offers a viable strategy for extracting genuine exoplanet atmospheric signals in the presence of stellar activity.

We present a novel approach to the arithmetic Arakel't method, which yields a curvature uniform metric $K$ on a compact Riemann surface $X$, where the metric remains singular at a designated finite set of points. This developed construction facilitates the formulation of a Lax pair for certain non-linear differential equations, specifically exemplified by the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) equation.

This study examines the mechanics of surface running in lightweight centipedes, specifically focusing on how they utilize a multi-legged system to prevent sinking and propel themselves across water. By analyzing the swimming behavior of a light specimen (0.08 g) and measuring the pressures exerted by individual legs during water contact, we reveal that the animal relies on specific legs to generate sinking-reducing pressure pulses for both sinking resistance and forward movement. Furthermore, the research establishes a correlation between the magnitude of these leg pressure pulses and the centipede's body mass, offering new insights into the specialized aquatic locomotion strategies of this low-weight organism.

Hydrodynamic simulations of the disperse, long-range propagation of a tsunami generated by a space body impact are typically modeled using a shallow water system. This study evaluates the suitability of the standard Boussinesq equations alongside the modified Boussinesq system, which accounts for finite depth, to accurately capture dispersive effects. The analysis proceeds by examining the dimensionless parameters inherent in the governing equations and the dimensionless solution structure of a point source. The findings indicate that the standard Boussinesq system, when applied to deep water regimes, fails to represent dispersive phenomena effectively. Conversely, the modified Boussinesq system, applicable to shallow water conditions, successfully captures dispersion. The study further notes that the degree of dispersive influence is contingent upon the dimensionless source strength.

We introduce the findings of the first Near-Infrared Reaching Through Space (RiRiTS) survey, which targets optically obscured infrared-bright galaxies at redshifts $0.3 < z < 0.8$. This study analyzes JWST NIRCam data for 100 targets previously identified as H-band non-detections in the Cosmic Assembly Near-Infrared Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey (CANDELS). Our results confirm that 60 of these sources are successfully detected by JWST, with redshifts ranging from $0.3 < z < 0.8$. These objects exhibit a median stellar mass of $\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) = 10.2 \pm 0.3$ and a median redshift of $z=0.5 \pm 0.1$. They are predominantly found in the central regions of the Great Observatories Second Quarter (COSMOS) field, situated within massive dark matter halos with $M_{200c} \gtrsim 10^{13} M_{\odot}$. This population represents a critical component of the cosmic star-forming mass density, accounting for approximately 20% of the total contribution at these redshifts. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between these galaxies and high-mass halos, suggesting that nearly all star formation in massive halos occurs in a form that remains optically hidden.

Building on the study of seven-dimensional Einstein-Maxwell theory with a magnetic flux, we incorporate the Chern-Simons action and a cosmological constant. The resulting equations of motion are solved to determine the geometry of the seven-dimensional spacetime. The general solution includes two arbitrary parameters, which are subsequently fixed by imposing the condition of finite energy. The paper concludes by discussing the physical attributes of the obtained solution.

This work examines the statistical mechanics of a one-dimensional model featuring hard-core interactions, consisting of disks of two distinct radii that cannot overlap and are confined within a channel of fixed width. We focus the analysis on the regime where the radius ratio approaches one, deriving exact results for the rank-one and rank-two alternating sequences to establish the phase diagram. Furthermore, we detail the behavior of disk and disk number density densities within each phase.

Non-affine behavior is a defining characteristic of glassy materials, where material displacement diverges from material deformation. We introduce an approach to quantify this phenomenon in soft condensed matter systems by measuring the angular distribution of scattered light. We demonstrate that the growth of the light's angular width during the softening regime of a colloidal crystal under shear offers a quantitative measure of non-affine behavior. We further establish that the ratio of the characteristic wavevectors for scattered light in this regime aligns with the ratio of total to affine displacement derived from molecular dynamics simulations of hard spheres. Additionally, we reveal that the angular distribution of light during shear-induced shear thickening in colloidal suspensions offers valuable insights into the non-affine dynamics responsible for this effect.

This study examines a single-species model characterized by age-structured dynamics, behavioral responses, and environmental pollution. We establish the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of positive bounded weak solutions that are regular within certain age intervals. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model admits a steady state which is both unique and globally stable across the entire system. Finally, we analyze how each model parameter influences population density across different age groups during steady states.

Taxonomy term embeddings are essential for numerous natural language processing tasks, including semantic search and information retrieval. While existing methods often rely on manual curation or heuristic rules to expand taxonomies, this research introduces HyperExpan, a machine learning-driven approach that automatically expands taxonomies by embedding them in a hyperbolic space. Leveraging the property of negative curvature in hyperbolic geometry allows HyperExpan to effectively model hierarchical relationships. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art taxonomy expansion techniques.

This study investigates how static electric fields affect the strength of non-covalent interactions in the S66 benchmark set, which comprises 65 π-π, hydrogen-bonding, and van der Waals complexes. We assessed field impacts by computing binding energies across various orientations using supermolecular methods combined with basis set superposition error (BSSE) corrections. Our analysis reveals that these fields generally alter interaction strengths by 5% to 10%, with notable exceptions for certain hydrogen-bonded pairs that exhibit significantly higher sensitivity. Additionally, we demonstrate that even modest fields can cause order-of-magnitude shifts in anisotropy values relative to field-free conditions. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating external fields when modeling non-covalent assemblies in environments subject to electrostatic influences.

This paper presents a novel uncertainty modelling approach for stochastic optimization within Industry 4.0 environments. By leveraging real-time data from connected cyber-physical systems, our method constructs a dynamic framework that captures uncertainty in real scheduling contexts. We demonstrate our approach using a real-world manufacturing scenario, where data from a connected machine and sensors are aggregated to develop a non-deterministic framework capable of addressing uncertainty through two distinct strategies: a deterministic method utilizing historical operational data, and a stochastic method based on historical data to characterize probability distributions. We evaluate these strategies using two benchmark problems—a single-machine scheduling problem and a job shop problem—finding that the deterministic approach is more effective for short-term scheduling, whereas the stochastic approach yields superior results for long-term scenarios.

This study establishes an framework grounded in Signal Temporal Logic (STL) to assess cyber-physical systems (CPS) for both current and anticipated resilience. We introduce a framework that unifies three key dimensions of resilience—robustness, adaptability, and recoverability—into a single quantifiable metric. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to integrate these three aspects of resilience into a cohesive measure. We also present a method for generating formal specifications that define the thresholds for each dimension, ensuring they collectively reflect the desired level of resilience. Furthermore, we provide a practical demonstration of this approach applied to a cyber-physical drone system.

We introduce a method for detecting dark matter in the sub-GeV mass range by analyzing data from accelerometer networks originally designed for gravitational wave research. Specifically, the dark matter-induced signals are identified through distinct temporal and spatial patterns in the results of a beam-former analysis. To validate this technique, we employed data from the LIGO and Virgo observatory networks, which have already been utilized for gravitational wave detection. Our study establishes that network-level analyses can reach sensitivities to accelerations as low as $0.15 \, \mu\text{m/s}^2$ for particle masses of 100 \, \text{MeV}/c^2. These performance levels are comparable to those anticipated from dedicated experiments utilizing slabs of test material.

We present a novel analysis of the Monger-Walker equation, originally proposed by Mardare and Wangar (2004), now examined within the framework of finite-dimensional Riemannian manifolds and through an entirely different approach. Specifically, we demonstrate that the equation's gradient can be approximated by solutions to the discrete-time system of parabolic PDEs, where the operator $|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u$ replaces the gradient term in a standard heat equation. The proof relies on the weak convergence of the associated functionals and their strong convergence on compact sets. The equation is also shown to possess a unique global solution that exists for all time and converges to a stationary solution as $t \to \infty$. The limiting solution corresponds to a harmonic function of degree $p$, which is a constant on a manifold with non-constant coefficients.

We present a statistical investigation of 1,015 faint radio sources (flux density $S_{1.4\rm{GHz}} = 0.5$–$5$ mJy) from the NVSS catalog, analyzing their properties via stacking techniques. These faint sources are statistically dominant in the radio sky, yet their individual characteristics remain poorly understood. By aggregating data from the sample, we detect a significant excess of emission around the positions of 1,015 NVSS sources relative to the surrounding control region. This stacked signal exhibits a Gaussian profile with a Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of $10.5 \pm 0.2$ arcsec, which translates to a physical size of approximately 100 kpc at an average redshift of 0.1. We further explore source characteristics—including redshift, luminosity, and morphology—using the stacking method. These analyses indicate that the majority of the sample consists of spiral galaxies, with the remaining fraction likely comprising radio-quiet AGN. Additionally, we establish a correlation between the slope of the spectral index and redshift, with steeper slopes observed in more distant objects.

Quantitative information management has become increasingly vital in recent years, particularly within the domain of quantitative information flows. This discipline addresses how to limit the disclosure of private data to adversaries. This study offers a generalized framework for analyzing such flow systems, extending beyond traditional hidden and obvious Markov models to incorporate broader stochastic structures. This broader class is termed "Abstract Hidden Markov Models" (AHMMs). An AHMM is defined by a probability measure representing the joint distribution of unobserved and observed data, constrained only by minimal structural assumptions. This flexibility makes AHMMs a versatile tool for modeling various flow scenarios. This work also provides a categorical interpretation of the AHMM framework, utilizing the theory of monads to formalize the relationship between hidden and observed data spaces. This approach yields an abstract formulation of the conditional expectation operator, which is crucial for calculating the information leakage between observations and latent variables. This generalized model encompasses classical Hidden Markov Models, as well as simpler stochastic processes like deterministic and random functions, under minimal structural constraints. Furthermore, the framework supports a monadic formulation of the do-calculus, enabling a generalized proof of do-callem rules and a formalization of quantitative information management principles. This provides a robust theoretical basis for analyzing and reasoning about information flow systems.

This work examines the nonlocal characteristics of the most unstable and the highly dissipative components within the temporal evolution of one-dimensional turbulence driven by periodic boundary conditions and nonlinear viscous forces. By analyzing the interaction between these regions, the study elucidates the mechanisms responsible for the emergence of the primary flow. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the primary flow is entirely determined by the statistical properties of these two regions, rendering the statistics of the remaining intermediate area irrelevant.

Scattering experiments serve as fundamental pillars for probing the natural world, yet their data analysis frequently relies on phenomenological models that are often too rigid to accommodate every conceivable outcome. We introduce a flexible scattering phenomenology that offers greater adaptability than traditional approaches. This framework is grounded in a universal, iterative algorithm designed to generate cross sections for arbitrary $2 \to 2$ scattering processes. By utilizing just four parameters, our method can effectively capture a broad spectrum of phenomena, including non-resonant effects. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to the $e^+e^- \to t\bar{c}$ process, highlighting its potential to explore new territory in particle physics research.

This work examines the thermal dynamics of a cavity under the combined influences of temperature and the Cavier effect. We investigate how the spectral energy density and specific heat capacity are modified when these factors coexist, building upon prior research. We identify that the modified Planck's law retains its fundamental structure, governed by the persistence of the speed of light as the maximum limit for light propagation velocity. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that when the Cavier effect is present, it becomes possible to derive modified versions of the Stefan-Boltzmann law and the Nernst–Thesis law.

To protect user confidentiality, location-based services (LBS) must rigorously safeguard user data. This study examines privacy within the context of a user's location history modeled as a sequence of independent positions drawn from an unknown distribution. We introduce the concept of $\epsilon$-conditional prior privacy, an extension of standard $\epsilon$-differential privacy. This new framework accounts for the fact that an adversary's potential knowledge regarding a user's history is not limited to a single data point but may encompass the entire underlying distribution. We demonstrate that this form of privacy is essential to guarantee security against a sophisticated adversary capable of exploiting prior distributional insights. We also establish a link between conditional prior privacy and an expanded version of exponential mechanism, which facilitates the design of differentially private algorithms tailored to initial distributional constraints. Finally, we apply these findings to a practical LBS scenario, demonstrating that both offline and online methods for generating privacy-preserving noisy locations under conditional prior privacy are more efficient than traditional differential privacy approaches.

Accurately positioning 3D environments is crucial for autonomous systems, particularly within the realm of self-driving cars. While the Normal Distribution Transform (NTT) representation has proven effective for this purpose, traditional Hough Voxel Feature (HVF)-based NTTs often rely on training with simulated data, which limits their real-world effectiveness. To address this, we introduce NDT-Transformer, a new end-to-end NTT-based localization framework that leverages large-scale 3D point cloud data. This approach replaces HVFs with a name-based local feature encoder utilizing a multi-head self-attention mechanism. By training the entire system in an end-to-end fashion, NDT-Transformer achieves superior real-world performance. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods, including a 20% increase in accurate localization compared to the previous best-in-class end-to-end NTT-Transformer variant.

Existing solutions have largely relied on absolute PE strategies, which are less than optimal for CMDS because word order is not always definitive due to borrowing patterns. This work introduces a novel approach that combines word-level and subword-level PEs with the addition of Relative PE to address word order ambiguities. Our experiments on three widely used CMDS demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms all baseline techniques.

Motion planning in dynamic settings is a critical challenge in robotics, particularly for autonomous vehicles. This work introduces a new method for creating spatio-temporal restriction maps to enhance motion planning performance within active environments. The approach leverages the temporal dimension to model spatio-temporal constraints, enabling a more precise forecasting of free space compared to static representations. To achieve this, we utilize a learned free space model based on a conditional variational auto-encoder (CVAE), which processes the recent history of free space to predict upcoming areas of movement. By distinguishing between occupied and free cells, the method generates restriction maps that guide motion planning algorithms. Experimental results across three distinct datasets demonstrate that the proposed strategy significantly improves planning performance relative to existing techniques.

This study introduces a novel approach to visual relocalization in 3D environments, designed to recover camera poses from novel views by leveraging both novel and previously seen visual cues within an integrated framework. We propose a new Surfel Map, enhanced with 3D geometry and enriched through a machine learning model trained to generate robust descriptors. These learned descriptors enable the system to effectively handle scenarios involving novel views, occlusions, and varying lighting conditions. We validate our methodology on the novel 3D indoor scene dataset, UCM-AirLand, demonstrating that our approach significantly surpasses the performance of the state-of-the-art, while also evaluating the system in a real-world scenario to verify its practical applicability.

This study introduces a multi-dimensional optimization framework designed to enhance performance in general multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (GUI-MIMO) systems. Our approach simultaneously determines the selection of active users for each base station antenna and the corresponding transmit precoding weights. By reformulating the joint problem as a group LASSO instance, we develop a computationally efficient algorithm that yields sparsity in the resulting precoding matrix. This sparsity leads to significant resource benefits, specifically by reducing the number of radio units allocated per user. Validated through extensive simulations using both standard and non-convex performance metrics, the results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively balances data transmission rates with unit allocation efficiency.

We have investigated the nematic instability in LiFeAs, a ferropnictide, by measuring the nematic susceptibility ($\chi_{nem}$) through the difference in resistivity along orthogonal axes. Our findings indicate that $\chi_{nem}$ increases with decreasing temperature, rising by a factor of 2.5 from 300 K to 20 K. This trend contradicts theoretical predictions for a nematic instability, which would require susceptibility to increase by a factor of 5 or 5.5 over the same temperature interval. These results suggest that LiFeAs does not exhibit a nematic instability.

Our analysis examines the model's sensitivity to potential deviations in the top quark and vector-like quark (VLQ) sectors, as well as their coupling to the Higgs boson. We determine the 95% confidence limits on the masses and couplings of the charged, neutral, and vector-like quark resonances, and we define the exclusion regions within their respective parameter spaces.

Anomaly-free chiral gauge theories are essential for constructing a consistent quantum framework. While the standard method for verifying anomaly cancellation involves summing contributions from all left- and right-handed fermion representations, this approach is computationally cumbersome for theories with numerous fermions. We introduce a robust algorithm that leverages the robustness of octaves to streamline these checks. Additionally, we examine the phases of general chiral gauge theories, identifying that they possess a non-trivial, non-local topological structure.

This study examines the direct dependency of solutions to the stationary Navier-Stokes equations on initial data within essential Besov spaces. We establish both existence and non-existence theorems, demonstrating that potential solutions may fail to exist for specific data, whereas unique local existence holds for other data within the same space. Additionally, we derive upper bounds regarding solution size and the distance between two distinct solutions, all dependent on the norm of the initial data. Finally, we illustrate that these existence theorems remain valid when the external force term is omitted.

We investigate the magnon spectrum within the high-temperature regime of antiferromagnetic materials, accounting for thermal equilibrium interactions with the lattice. Our findings indicate that magnons experience a redshift in their frequency due to a nonlinear mechanism driven by the nonlinear susceptibility of the lattice, while simultaneously undergoing squeezing—a phenomenon where uncertainty is reduced in one variable but amplified in its conjugate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the efficiency of both spectral shift and thermal squeezing escalates as the temperature rises. These predictions align with recent experimental findings regarding magnon linewidths and uncertainty bounds in Cr₂O₃, thereby offering a theoretical foundation for the observed data.

This study introduces two modifications to Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, which relies on codes with a low relative dimension within a larger extension field. Our findings indicate that while increasing the underlying code's size enhances security, this approach also proportionately raises the costs associated with encryption and decryption.

Pre-training has emerged as a foundational technique for developing effective language models. While recent studies have begun integrating external knowledge sources, such as knowledge graphs, into the pre-training process, these efforts remain limited. This paper proposes a novel approach, named Dict-BERT, which enhances the standard BERT pre-training objective by incorporating data from a thesaurus dictionary. This addition serves to enrich the model with semantic information, thereby boosting its ability to discern fine-grained word meanings. Experiments conducted on various sentence-level classification tasks demonstrate that our dictionary-enhanced BERT model achieves performance comparable to or exceeding that of recent state-of-the-art variants.

This work investigates the limiting distributions of the mean weight (mass) and the heaviest and lightest edges in the minimal spanning acycles of random simplicial complexes, which are defined by a birth process for $k$-simplices governed by a probability function $p$. These acycles serve as combinatorial analogues to persistence diagrams, which are used in topological data analysis to characterize the shape of data via persistent homology. We establish that the mass converges to a normal distribution, while the edges at the weight extremes approach Gumbel distributions. Our findings hold for a broad range of $p$, encompassing both the regime where Betti numbers grow polynomially and the regime where they expand exponentially with vertex count $n$. Notably, our results extend previous findings on persistence homology extremes by Fuster, Mémoli, and Scott, which were limited to cases where $p$ approaches 1 sufficiently rapidly.

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) has garnered significant interest as a privacy-preserving technique for data analysis. Nevertheless, numerous VFL privacy vulnerabilities have been identified, and the current state of research often relies on simplified models that fail to accurately represent real-world VFL environments. This paper introduces two novel attacks against VFL: a gradient reconstruction attack and a gradient mask attack. The former enables adversaries to reconstruct private data from model gradients, while the latter allows the extraction of information without physical access to the data. These attacks are demonstrated to be effective within authentic VFL settings. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the attack mechanisms and discuss potential defensive strategies to counter them.

Using light-cone sum rules, we calculate the hadronic matrix elements for a two-body exclusive $B$-meson decay involving a baryon-antibaryon final state (specifically $B \to pp^{\prime}$, where $p$ denotes a proton and $\mathcal{D}$ denotes a dark baryon). We find that these matrix elements are governed by the twist-3 dark baryon light-cone distribution amplitude (DA), with power-suppressed contributions from twist-2 and twist-4 amplitudes. To address the renormalization group evolution of the dark DA, we derive the corresponding evolution equations. Furthermore, we establish q̃ (quarkonium) sum rules to determine its momentum sum rule and determine its DA at the scale matching the $B$-meson, $\mu_0 = m_B$. Finally, we apply these results to a concrete model demonstrating how to extract the Wilson coefficient for $B \to p\bar{\mathcal{D}}$ transitions.

This paper introduces Intelligent City Defense Game, a framework designed to model the strategic resource management required to defend Socio-Cyber-Physical Systems (SCPS) during attacks. The Intelligent City Defense Game adapts the City Defense Game model by incorporating the influence of intelligent agents on both the cyber and physical dimensions of SCPS. We define an SCPS as a network of cyber systems that control physical systems, which are further managed by agents possessing their own objectives and distinct levels of vulnerability to cyber intrusions. These systems are governed by two player types: the Defender, tasked with protecting the city, and the Attacker, whose goal is to inflict maximum damage. Defender actions include deploying resources to safeguard nodes and the Reconnaissance action, which reveals the current knowledge of the Defender regarding the Attacker's capabilities and intentions. The objective of the Defender is to maximize the security of the city while minimizing expenditure, whereas the Attacker aims to maximize damage output while minimizing resource costs. We establish the formal properties of the game, including the role of the Defender's knowledge level, and demonstrate that the game possesses the crucial characteristic of being "no-regret." This property ensures that both players can achieve their respective goals without needing to express regret over their strategic choices. Finally, we present a solution method based on the "no-regret" attribute, enabling both players to learn optimal strategies through repeated interactions.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are highly effective for learning node representations, yet they typically depend on numerous labels. This requirement is often impractical, as gathering labels is costly and time-consuming. Few-shot learning offers a promising solution by utilizing a vast training pool and restricting labeled data to specific target classes. Previous approaches in this area have primarily focused on generating pseudo-tags to augment labeled samples. However, these methods frequently suffer from noisy pseudo-tagging and inefficient use of pseudo-labels. This paper introduces a new framework featuring a dual-stage model that enhances pseudo-tagging accuracy and optimally leverages pseudo-labels. In the initial phase, we employ a graph-based encoder to derive informative node embeddings. Subsequently, in the second phase, we apply a multi-label classifier to generate pseudo-labels. Experimental results across three public datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot node classification tasks.

CERN's AWAKE experiment aims to demonstrate plasma wakefield acceleration, a promising method for significantly boosting proton beam luminosity in future colliders. During this process, intense betatron radiation is emitted by electrons oscillating within the plasma. This paper details the simulation of betatron emission using the open-source betatron emission code BETARAD, which was employed to analyze emission characteristics across various plasma densities and laser phase offsets. The study highlights how these parameters influence the angular distribution of radiation and identifies specific spectral peaks resulting from the Doppler effect. Furthermore, it notes that for plasma densities exceeding a critical threshold, the spectral composition shifts, with the upper limit of emitted photon energy becoming governed by quantum electrodynamic (QED) effects.

Differentially private distributed decision tree (DPT) learning is a vital technique for protecting data privacy in machine learning. This paper presents a new approach that is both scalable and rigorously proven to maintain privacy. Our method employs a specialized Pruning-based algorithm that is more efficient than the standard approach of simply adding noise to the data. Our results demonstrate that our method is not only more efficient than the standard approach of simply adding noise to the data, but also achieves a significant improvement in accuracy.

This study addresses cases where a channel is specified via a Renyi divergence metric rather than a traditional probability mass function. We propose a proximal gradient algorithm to compute the channel estimate that minimizes the Renyi divergence between the empirical mass function of observed outputs and this mass function representing the channel. To ensure convergence, we employ a regularized variant of Renyi divergence and establish a convergence rate of $O(1/t)$ for the regularized objective value. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a regularized objective value falling below a predetermined threshold is guaranteed within a specific number of iterations, provided the regularized minimum is known. We validate these theoretical findings with numerical experiments on a binary symmetric channel scenario.

Chain event graph (ChEV) model selection is introduced as a novel approach within Bayesian network (BN) systems to handle sequential decision-making processes. Unlike conventional methods, this framework treats ChEVs as distinct generators for deterministic Bayesian networks, thereby allowing the direct incorporation of topological constraints into the BN inference. By embedding the prior probability directly into the model's Bayes factor, topological restrictions are effectively regularized the prior distribution. Consequently, the selection of an optimal ChEV structure is resolved through maximum a posteriori probability (MAP) estimation of the corresponding BN generator, and a detailed derivation of this procedure is provided.

This work examines the asymptotic behavior of damped inertial dynamics incorporating Tikhonov regularization applied to the minimization of $\mu$-convex functions. When the regularization and Tikhonov parameters both vanish over time, the dynamics yield an inertial trajectory that converges to the minimum norm solution. By selecting a specific pair of parameters, the rate of convergence can be accelerated. Under mild assumptions, the exponential rate of convergence is achieved if the function is essentially strongly convex; otherwise, for essential strict convexity, the rate of divergence depends on the modulus of convexity.

This paper investigates the inherent disorderly nature of phase transitions in single-agent, single-phenomenon systems, specifically focusing on wall-following robots. We introduce a novel agent-based model designed to replicate the emergent, self-sustained oscillations of these phases observed in line-forming robots. Our results demonstrate that the absence of explicit inter-agent communication is sufficient to produce complex behaviors characteristic of multi-agent ensembles. Furthermore, we reveal that the resulting oscillations are spatially heterogeneous, manifesting as coexisting regions of distinct phases within the same system. This discovery underscores the potential for significant behavioral variability in individual, isolated robots. Finally, we illustrate that this phenomenon serves as a highly sensitive indicator of the system's parameters, such as those related to the phase change, making it a valuable metric for such characteristics.

A self-consistent approach is employed to investigate the impact of extended impurities on the kinetic-energy-driven superconductivity observed in cuprates. The study focuses on an anisotropic SC state characterized by a gap structure that features nodes along diagonals but exhibits suppressed gap magnitude near the zone boundary. The primary focus examines the low-temperature microwave conductivity within the dirty limit regime for both nonmagnetic and magnetically active impurity cases. The findings indicate that the kinetic-energy-driven superconductivity remains robust against nonmagnetic impurities. However, magnetic impurities are shown to significantly suppress the kinetic-energy-driven critical temperature. The study further explores the implications of these findings regarding the nature of superconductivity in iron-poor cuprates.

This text offers a concise introduction to a less explored crystalline curvature movement process. The standard motion governed by crystalline curvature is defined as the level set evolution determined by the $L^1$-convolution of the mean curvature measure, a concept first formalized by Caffarelli, Monneau, and Morabito in 2017. In contrast, this survey examines a broader variant in which the convolution integral applies to the total curvature rather than the mean curvature. The authors trace the origins of this concept to a 1997 study by Caffarelli and Friedman and detail its connection to curvature flows driven by anisotropic surface tensions. Furthermore, the paper details specific crystallization phenomena and characterizes the corresponding crystallization curvatures along with their associated evolution equations.

Plants are essential for human life, yet growing them successfully demands specific knowledge. To address this, we introduce GrowSpace, a virtual simulation designed to help users master plant cultivation. Within this environment, users manage a shared resource pool to apply actions like watering, fertilizing, and exposing plants to light. A plant's survival and growth depend on applying these actions correctly based on its specific requirements. Our primary goal is to develop a simulation that is both challenging and efficient to create, enabling learners to acquire cultivation skills through rapid experimentation and iteration. Our findings demonstrate that GrowSpace effectively teaches core concepts of plant biology, making it a valuable tool for users to experiment with plant growth in real-world scenarios.

Image biomarkers serve as quantitative measures of a disease or its treatment, and their growing importance in medical research has fostered a community of image-based quantitative methods. These efforts have generated a wide array of algorithms and tools, though the lack of standardized protocols hinders consistent application and limits the ability to compare findings across different studies. To address this, the Image Biomarker Markmatrices Initiative (IBNI) was established to develop standardized workflows for image analysis biomarkers in clinical settings. This document outlines the progress made during its first four years. IBNI has formed working groups to evaluate specific biomarkers, review existing literature, and identify necessary standardization steps. Additionally, the Initiative has launched public forums for algorithm submission and testing, facilitating a standardized environment for evaluating image analysis methods through a benchmarking process.

This study examines the influence of the $\Delta$ resonance and high-spin nucleon resonances on $K\Lambda$ and $K\pi$ photo-production mechanisms. Utilizing a relativistic dynamical framework grounded in chiral effective field theory, the $\Delta$ resonance is incorporated within a coupled-channel baryon-meson interaction channel. The derived $D_{3/5/2-}$ couplings to the $\pi N$ system are subsequently applied to $K\pi$ photo-production calculations. Results indicate that the $D_{3/5/2-}$ resonances exert a negligible impact on the $K\pi$ photo-production process. Furthermore, the study explores the sensitivity of $K\pi$ photo-production to the electromagnetic form factors of the $\Delta$ resonance, which are constrained by $K\pi$ photo-production off the $\pi N$ system. The findings suggest that the $K\pi$ photo-production process offers a viable avenue for determining the $\Delta$ resonance's electromagnetic form factors.
