This paper outlines a natural language processing approach designed to identify the development drivers of autonomous swarm systems used in military applications. We introduce a dataset comprising 100 research articles covering various development factors, alongside a method for rating the significance of specific drivers based on dataset analysis. Additionally, we employ a graph neural network to assess how these drivers interconnect with one another.

We introduce a methodology to derive cosmological parameters directly from the three-dimensional correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, bypassing the need to fit the distribution to theoretical models. This approach utilizes the "peak of the mean transmission" (PMT), a statistic defined as the average maximum transmission across quasar pairs at a fixed separation. The PMT is sensitive to the comoving distance between quasars, which in turn depends on cosmological variables. By analyzing the PMT's behavior over a range of distances, we can constrain these parameters. Our analysis of SDSS BOSS data yields a Hubble constant of $H_0 = 68.1 \pm 1.9$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and a matter density parameter of $\Omega_{m0} = 0.28 \pm 0.05$, with results remaining consistent when varying the redshift distribution of the quasars. This method offers a straightforward and robust means of measuring cosmological variables directly from the large-scale structure of the universe.

Emittance serves as a critical metric for characterizing the quality of a particle accelerator beam. While the transport of longitudinal emittance is well-understood, achieving the same for the transverse variant is more difficult due to coupling mechanisms. This work presents, for the first time, the experimental confirmation of transverse emittance transfer between beam lines, alongside the measurement of the longitudinal emittance transfer. These findings were achieved using two specialized sections of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC): Section 5, which functions as a cryogenic test area, and Section 6, equipped with new wire-based emittance measurement systems. The results offer valuable insights for future efforts to transfer emittance in standard physics colliders.

This study introduces a new sliding-window mechanism designed to enhance trajectory prediction. It involves iteratively re-evaluating all intermediate trajectories within the sliding window and applying the final prediction based on the aggregated outcomes of these re-evaluations. Furthermore, a Social Awareness Evaluation (SAE) module is developed to assess the social plausibility of trajectories that lack societal awareness. This module employs a social-awareness encoder to extract contextual information from other agents and a social-awareness decoder to regenerate the contextual features embedded in the original trajectories. The primary function of the SAE module is to evaluate the alignment between a specific trajectory and the surrounding context, thereby guiding the re-evaluation process. Additionally, a social-awareness loss function is formulated to train the SAE module effectively. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed prediction system achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.

This paper investigates the complexity of discrete Boltzmann machines by applying information-theoretic metrics, including Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance, mutual information (MI), and coefficient determination (R²). We analyze how network size, temperature, and training influence these complexity measures. Our findings reveal a clear trend: as the KS distance increases with higher temperature and network size, it consistently declines for smaller systems and lower thermal levels. Regarding mutual information, it rises with temperature up to a specific threshold before decreasing, and it is similarly temperature-sensitive in smaller architectures. The R² coefficient, conversely, behaves inversely to the KS distance, rising with temperature and system size while remaining lower in broader contexts at cool states.

Beyond observation, we explore the relationship between these metrics and the intrinsic properties of Boltzmann machines. Our analysis suggests that these information-theoretic indicators effectively capture the topological structure and weight distributions of the networks. Consequently, they emerge as valuable tools for assessing model complexity, guiding hyperparameter selection, and enhancing the interpretability of Boltzmann machines in practical applications.

The rapid development of robotics has made human-swarm interaction (HSI) a critical research domain. While current HSI systems are mostly centralized, necessitating a human operator to control the entire swarm from a dedicated station, this paper introduces a decentralized paradigm. Our approach enables individuals to guide specific robots within a multi-robot group using hand gestures. We validate this concept through an experiment involving three Khepera III robots, where participants issued one of eight distinct Chinese hand signals to direct the actions of a targeted unit. We also present a sequential deep learning algorithm capable of identifying these signs with 86.6% accuracy. These findings offer valuable insights for next-generation decentralized control frameworks driven by human input.

This study introduces an optimized architecture for classifying blood cells, built by integrating two distinct Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): the first utilizes raw RGB imagery, while the second processes RGB images enhanced with edge information. Merging their respective outputs via a fully-connected layer and training this combined model on the BD Multisite dataset yielded 98.5% accuracy, outperforming single-model approaches. This gap highlights the advantage of the dual-cascade design, which combines RGB analysis with edge-based feature detection.

Counterdiabatic (CD) techniques offer an effective means to initialize ground states by accelerating adiabatic evolution. While adding explicit CD terms often incurs prohibitive overhead, variational counterdiabatic (VCD) approaches offer a practical solution by approximating these terms using parameterized Hamiltonians optimized via variational principles. This study examines the VCD method applied to initializing the ground state of the Hubbard model on bipartite lattices. We evaluate various parameterized ansatzes, including those based on Jordan-Wigner strings, spin operators, and fermionic modes. Our results indicate that for small system sizes, the most efficient ansatzs are derived from Jordan-Wigner formulations. Additionally, we assess the impact of different variational optimization strategies, including stochastic gradient descent, the BFGS algorithm, and the Krotosch method.

This work introduces a novel color temperature-based approach to detect and mitigate shifting white balance during video discoloration. By integrating a specialized version of the Beyer pseudo-trichromatic model with a new quantification of color temperature, the method achieves rapid performance, making it well-suited for real-time tone processing. The algorithm's effectiveness in both discoloration detection and correction has been validated through experiments on diverse datasets, yielding promising results. Furthermore, the proposed solution demonstrates significant advantages over existing techniques in specific scenarios. The open-source MATLAB implementation can be accessed at:

We introduce the Exponential Taylor Expansion, a novel approach to function approximation that employs a new type of basis function designed to resolve challenges where traditional Taylor series fail, addressing the limitations of classical methods.

Laser-plasma interactions offer a versatile platform for generating intense photon beams, thereby establishing a comprehensive research framework for exploring photon-photon collisions within a laboratory context. This article reviews the primary mechanisms for laser-plasma photonization, emphasizing those suitable for designing experimental setups to study these collisions. Furthermore, it examines various proposals for photon circularization, including the generation of polarized light, and assesses the potential for creating high-energy photon sources. Finally, the photon collision cross sections are analyzed alongside predicted laboratory signals, with a specific focus on the generation of X-ray and gamma-ray emission pairs.

This study examines the sensitivity of the Higgs coupling modification factor $\kappa_Z$ to the 2HDM soft-breaking parameter $m_{12}$, alongside the associated theoretical constraints and physical implications. We find that the Higgs mass, the $Z$-boson mass, and the Higgs self-couplings exhibit varying degrees of dependence on $m_{12}$, with self-couplings showing the highest sensitivity. While electroweak precision data impose strict upper limits on $m_{12}$, allowing it to be neglected in many contexts, specific regions of parameter space permit values large enough to induce significant deviations in the Higgs self-couplings.

To address challenges associated with RDF schema validation, W3C has developed ShEx and Shacl. These tools enable the definition of concrete formats for validating RDF graphs. This work introduces a framework designed to transfer data between relational and RDF representations, accounting for these shape expressions. The core of this research lies in an intermediate framework that abstracts away the specific syntax differences of each language. We examine how different relational semantics—tubular versus entity-relationship—map to corresponding RDF model representations. Furthermore, we outline a general approach for transforming between any abstractly defined model and graph structures. Finally, the study outlines the complexities and inherent difficulties inherent in such transformations.

Convex regression and frontier estimation represent two closely linked fields that address critical challenges in economics, business, and finance. Although these areas have a long history, the advent of high-performance computing has recently made them more accessible to researchers. This paper introduces `pyStoNED`, a new Python toolkit designed to facilitate the implementation of frontier estimation models and convex regression techniques. We provide a detailed overview of the package's capabilities, supported by examples that include both simulated data and real-world datasets.

We introduce a new method for discovering the SM-like Higgs boson within a two-Higgs doublet framework via $t \bar t \phi$ production at the LHC. This approach leverages the substantial mass difference between the decaying particle and the stable, weakly interacting partners, which results in a distinctive kinematic signature. The analysis indicates that the technique remains effective across a broad spectrum of model parameters, covering a mass range from 500 GeV down to approximately 150 GeV. Furthermore, the method demonstrates resilience against uncertainties in the direct search limits for the channel $pp \to t \bar t \phi$.

We introduce a straightforward technique for distilling task-specific knowledge into unsupervised and few-shot settings directly from a frozen, pretrained language model. This method involves fine-tuning a smaller auxiliary model on data sampled from the larger one, followed by utilizing that auxiliary model for tasks such as unsupervised and few-shot learning. Experiments conducted on COT (a collection of 11 diverse datasets) and the UFER framework demonstrate that this approach is highly efficient, yielding performance comparable to or superior to current state-of-the-art methods with minimal overhead. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between domain similarity and sample quantity in few-shot scenarios, offering new insights into how these factors influence results within the few-shot framework.

The analysis incorporates multi-epoch spectroscopic data to characterize their properties. Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is a critical component of automated telephone systems. While data-driven approaches have recently achieved significant success, acquiring sufficiently large datasets remains a significant hurdle. This paper introduces a novel strategy to augment training data for ITN, specifically targeting scenarios with limited sample sizes. The method involves applying various transformations to existing numerical representations. Experimental results demonstrate that this augmentation technique yields substantial performance gains, particularly within the domain of numeric ITN. The study further confirms the method's versatility by evaluating it on a broader range of tasks, including those involving dates and times. The accompanying source code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/rohanagarwal123/itn_data_augmentation}.

This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn inequality concerning the first eigenvalue of the Hermitian operator subject to a Robin boundary condition on a smooth, strictly convex submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Additionally, a corresponding result is demonstrated for the Hermitian operator under a Dirichlet boundary condition. As natural consequences, we derive corresponding Theorems for the first eigenvalues of both Robin and Dirichlet problems.

Non-Exchangeable Types (NFTs) are introduced as a new class of dependent and heterogeneous data-dependent type, extending the exchangeability-based type theory to accommodate dependent types that vary across units. This framework enables precise probabilistic reasoning for modern data structures characterized heterogeneity and dependency. To achieve this, a novel NFT-kernel is defined to facilitate the construction of NFTs, and corresponding proofs for soundness and completeness are provided. These theoretical results demonstrate that the proposed type system can accurately model heterogeneous and dependent structures while maintaining rigorous statistical inference.

While non-Hermitian systems have been extensively studied in one dimension, the impact of correlations on their topological properties remains poorly understood. This study examines the reduction of point-gap topology in chiral-symmetric non-Hermitian fermion models caused by fermion fractionalization and the associated finite-size effects. We demonstrate that, contrary to expectations in Hermitian systems, correlation functions in these non-Hermitian frameworks can exhibit non-trivial spatial profiles. Furthermore, we establish that in the thermodynamic limit, the bulk behavior of non-Hermitian systems with fermionic symmetry can be accurately captured by mapping them onto equivalent Hermitian systems with altered chiralities. These findings offer valuable insights into the topological dynamics of correlated non-Hermitian matter.

We introduce a straightforward technique for embedding social speaker traits into synthetic speech by adjusting the acoustic characteristics of existing models. Utilizing a pre-trained speaker customization system, we fine-tune it using acoustic embeddings derived from a speaker exhibiting the target trait. This method produces high-fidelity customized speech without requiring any initial optimization. Furthermore, we assess the efficacy of this approach across various traits, including age, gender, and accent, demonstrating its versatility in modifying synthetic speech.

We introduce a radiative seesaw framework featuring three right-handed neutrinos organized into an $A_4$ triplet, which spontaneously breaks the modular $\Gamma_3$ symmetry to yield residual $\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_3 \times Z_2$ factors. This model also incorporates the dark photon sector, consisting of a dark $U(1)_D$ gauge symmetry and a dark Higgs doublet. The dark sector communicates with the visible sector via a portal coupling mediated by a scalar doublet, linking it to the Standard Model. The dark symmetry is broken at an intermediate scale by a scalar field, thereby generating the dark photon mass. The model's parameters are fixed by the neutrino mass matrix, mixing angles, and CP phases, alongside the dark photon mass. Notably, neutrino masses and mixing angles dictate the $Z_2$ dark matter candidate's mass, offering a testable prediction for dark matter. The model demonstrates compatibility with current experimental constraints and neutrino oscillation data.

This paper investigates the collective dynamics of triaxial nuclei, specifically ${}^{152}\text{Dy}$ and ${}^{154}\text{Dy}$, by applying the extended finite temperature interacting boson approximation (EBIBM2). Within this framework, the uncertainty principle is modified to incorporate a minimum length scale, a feature designed to address the singularities found in the potential field associated with nuclear deformation. The study analyzes thermally induced phase transitions, examining both static electric quadrupole moments ($B(E2)$) and dynamic parameters, including triaxiality, energy levels, and transition rates. The results indicate that incorporating a minimal length scale significantly impacts ground-state phase transitions, quadrupole moments, and dynamic collective properties.

Detecting changes in remote sensing imagery is crucial for monitoring environmental shifts, such as urban development and deforestation. While deep learning has proven effective for change detection in high-dimensional hyperspectral images (HSI), most existing methods rely on fully supervised training, which is costly and impractical for large-scale datasets. These features are then integrated through a feature fusion mechanism, which employs two 2D CM networks to generate a comprehensive change map. The framework's efficacy is validated on three real-world HSI datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to both supervised and unsupervised counterparts.

We explore a cyclic cosmological framework that naturally accommodates the $\Lambda$CDM paradigm. In this model, dark energy is a transient feature of the cyclic process, while dark matter and the standard cosmological parameters remain inherent and consistent with current observations. Furthermore, the approach offers a theoretical basis for cosmic acceleration and provides an elegant explanation for the coincidence problem.

The Invariant-set theory, superdeterministic in nature, posits that quantum mechanics emerges from a classical system governed by a novel conservation law. We have developed a hidden-variable model capable of replicating the double-slit experiment, the single-particle version thereof, quantum entanglement, the corresponding Bell's inequality, and von Neumann's first and second attacks. Our findings demonstrate that the model successfully accounts for all statistical outcomes observed in these experiments.

Keyphrase detection, or the Keyphrase Spotting (KPS) task, involves identifying concise textual descriptions within articles. Traditionally, the computationally intensive deep neural networks (DNNs) required for accurate KPS execution demand significant processing power, rendering them unsuitable for the low-resource, text-centric text-streaming applications on the edge, such as IoT devices. This study introduces a strategy to adapt these heavy DNNs for deployment on resource-constrained edge hardware. Specifically, we examine the impact of three critical factors: model quantization, knowledge distillation, and knowledge compression. Our findings indicate that quantization offers the most effective balance between maintaining model performance and reducing computational overhead.

The paper investigates the critical dimer model placed within a background gauge field, characterized by complex weights assigned to the graph's edges. It is demonstrated that the critical partition function corresponds to a Dirac fermion one-loop determinant characterized by a 2D Dirac fermion moving in a background gauge and scalar field. In the case of a pure gauge field, the result recovers the 2D level-zero Polyakov formula. Furthermore, for the case of an associated scalar field, a novel scalar field potential is identified which permits an exact determination of the full path integral.

This paper introduces a novel strategy for identifying groups within high-dimensional categorical data, subsequently utilizing these groups to execute variable selection. While standard variable selection methods often rely on continuous data and standard Lasso techniques to handle sparsity, our approach is designed specifically for discrete, categorical contexts. We first cluster the distinct categories into coherent groups, then apply a modified Group Lasso algorithm that incorporates additional regularization to promote sparsity. This integrated workflow is validated through extensive simulations and real-world data analysis, demonstrating the method's effectiveness.

To address the escalating need for mixed-criticality embedded systems, this paper presents a new T-Visor architecture leveraging advanced hardware virtualization capabilities. Built upon the virtualization engine of an Intel-based ARM architecture, this T-Visor manages multiple virtual platforms, allowing direct execution of both bare-metal applications and Linux on isolated hardware environments. Designed to minimize overhead, the system achieves significant performance: virtualization incurs less than a 1% penalty for real-time tasks and less than 5% penalty for Linux workloads. Furthermore, the architecture supports flexible configuration, enabling the addition of further virtual platforms or bare-metal domains alongside existing ones.

Solving the panoramic stitching problem involves determining a set of camera poses and image warps that align overlapping views. This paper introduces a novel, two-stage pipeline designed to find the minimal warping required to merge these images. Initially, we employ a pose estimation algorithm to derive a gravity-aligned reference for each camera. Subsequently, we apply a panoramic stitching method that respects this gravity prior, thereby constraining the resulting camera orientations. Experimental results on both synthetic data and real-world imagery demonstrate that our two-step approach yields significantly more compact solutions than existing stitching techniques that lack gravity constraints.

This study investigates the synchronization dynamics of identical, weakly coupled oscillators influenced by uniform random fluctuations. We present a theoretical framework that accounts for the coexistence of synchronized and desynchronized states and aligns well with both computational simulations and experimental data. Specifically, we examine a chimera state in which the population splits into a coherent group and an incoherent group, with the transition boundaries between these states being defined by the magnitudes of random fluctuations.

Robotic control is fundamentally about managing a dynamic system to achieve specific goals, yet this task becomes highly complex when dealing with uncertainties in perception, system dynamics, and action execution. While traditional methods often rely on predefined, hand-crafted rules to handle these uncertainties, the resulting controllers tend to be rigid and lack the flexibility required for real-world scenarios. This study addresses the challenge of learning effective regulators for dynamic systems subject to significant uncertainty. We propose a novel model-based reinforcement learning approach that utilizes probabilistic transition estimates to identify robust control policies. Specifically, the objective is to minimize the expected cost over a finite horizon, accounting for substantial uncertainty in the reward function and all probabilistic elements within the state transition model. By employing uncertainty-aware planning, the proposed method yields robust policies that remain effective despite uncertainty. We establish a polynomial sample complexity bound for the learning process and develop an uncertainty-aware planning algorithm that guarantees near-optimal performance. Empirical evaluations on various robotic control tasks demonstrate the method's ability to generate robust policies that outperform existing approaches.

To generalize May's operad of higher slice algebras, we introduce the concept of colored higher slice algebras, which are governed by the higher slice multigraph comonoid defined in [BS21]. We establish a biadjunction between these higher slice algebras and precollections of higher slice diagrams as formulated in [BSW]. Building on the multi-layer diagram approach from [SW], we further demonstrate that there exists an equivalence preserving this structure: colored higher slice algebras are equivalent to multi-layer diagrams organized into a higher category.

Random tensor networks (RTNs) serve as compelling candidates for the study of average-case scenarios in quantum chaos and holography. We introduce a new class of RTNs constructed from $U(N)$ matrices, featuring a boundary of $2\log N$ and a central geodesic that divides the geometry symmetrically. When a two-point correlation function is evaluated across this separated geodesic, the resulting data exhibits a distinct dependence on the crossing distance, an effect that becomes prominent in the region of large $U(N)$ dimensions. We demonstrate that this behavior mirrors predictions made by geodesic dual quantum circuits possessing a specific entanglement Hamiltonian. Furthermore, by calculating the second moment of the ground state energy, we confirm that it aligns with the standard prediction of $\langle E_0^2\rangle = \frac{\pi^2}{8}$.

Although living cells are inherently noisy, they successfully navigate random fluctuations to achieve specific goals. A critical unresolved issue is how cells effectively harness this randomness to generate diverse, intricate, and diverse functional outcomes. This study examines a fundamental challenge: how can cells reliably extract heritable data from transient, noise-driven dynamics? We demonstrate that even in systems lacking a stable fixed point, specific initial conditions can lead to non-trivial, self-averaging temporal patterns that endure across generations. These enduring patterns define a computable metric for the underlying information contained within stochastic dynamics. We further establish that both the magnitude of internal noise and external variability can significantly amplify this stored information. Consequently, robust non-equilibrium behaviors emerge as a viable mechanism for transmitting critical heritable data through cellular divisions.

This work explores a parametric family of three-dimensional Hénon-like dynamical models. By analyzing the influence of parameters on the dynamics, we identify regions of parameter values that yield chaotic attractors, which we visualize using both cross-sectional and full three-dimensional representations.

We demonstrate that the holonomy of a flat connection within an affine bundle over a manifold, when restricted to its action on the space of covariant vectors, can only exist as a single global differential equation. This result stands as a fresh proof of the uniqueness theorem regarding solutions to Einstein's equations in the context of the absolute parallelism (AP) formalism. This approach also establishes the equivalence between finding a $\mathrm{AP}$ connection that yields a flat target space and identifying a specific flat connection on the associated vector bundle. Such findings have significant consequences for the classification of flat spaces and the analysis of seven-dimensional $G_2$-structure manifolds.

The leading-twist distribution functions for vector and pseudoscalar P-wave mesons are derived using the QCD light-cone expansion applied to the corresponding Euclidean correlation functions. By employing a rigorous four-dimensional sum rule analysis, we determine the leading-twist distribution amplitudes of these P-wave mesons at a renormalization scale of $\mu_0=1$ GeV. The calculated results demonstrate that the shapes of the resulting distributions are in good agreement with those predicted by the nonrelativistic quark model.

The text describes investigating a nonlinear quantum scalar field within $1+1$ dimensions, focusing on its behavior as a Bose-Einstein condensate. It examines the ground state properties defined by nonlinear interactions and operators that alter these characteristics. Additionally, it analyzes the creation and annihilation operators associated with the condensate and their link to quantum field theory, while also exploring the field's spatial and temporal evolution.

The asymptotic symmetries of Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) spacetime have been identified as a potential framework for characterizing the infrared sector of scattering processes in asymptotically flat four-dimensional spaces. This perspective offers a novel interpretation of established physical principles, such as energy conservation, angular momentum conservation, and the Kac-Ward formula, by mapping them onto specific asymptotic symmetries and their corresponding Ward identities. Furthermore, it elucidates soft theorems, including soft photon and graviton theorems, as direct consequences of these very same symmetries. This discussion also addresses recent developments in three-dimensional asymptotically flat geometries, where the role of BMS geometry in soft theorems is examined.

This research addresses the challenge of online ensemble learning in a continual setting, where data streams through successive, non-recoverable task sequences. The objective is to develop an adaptive method capable of learning from incoming data while maintaining performance across all previously encountered tasks. To this end, we introduce ONESCEL, a neural ensemble model that combines task-specific subnetworks with task-shared layers. This architecture facilitates the simultaneous acquisition of new information and the preservation of past knowledge. We also present ONESCEL-T, a streamlined variant of ONESCEL that further enhances performance by integrating task identification and adaptive sampling. Comprehensive evaluations on various online continual learning benchmarks demonstrate that our models significantly outperform existing solutions.

Recent research has highlighted forms equipped with generalized metrics, characterized by the presence of a tensor possessing specific symmetry and vanishing divergence properties. We demonstrate that these structures can be interpreted as the restriction of the general (weak) Calabi-Yau definition to real manifolds. Furthermore, we prove that any generalized form satisfying these requirements allows for the creation of generalized measure structures. Specifically, in dimensions four, we identify a canonical Ricci-flat four-measure derived from any closed four-form.

A polynomial $f(x) \in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ is classified as a permutation polynomial over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ if the mapping $x \mapsto f(x)$ induces a bijection on the elements of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$. This study introduces a polynomial $f(x) \in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ that permutes elements within the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$ and demonstrates that the collection of all such polynomials forms a monoid under standard polynomial addition. Furthermore, the text establishes the conditions under which $x \mapsto f(x + a) + b$ acts as a bijection on the additive group $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$ for any $a, b \in \mathbb{F}_{q^3}$, noting that this specific property also defines a commuting subring within the ring of all polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$. The research provides explicit characterizations for both the ring and a commuting subset of total permutation polynomials over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$.

Intestinal parasites are a major cause of illness and death, particularly in developing nations. While medical professionals typically identify these conditions by examining microscopic samples from stool, the process is often arduous, time-consuming, and prone to errors. This study introduces a new method for automating the classification of intestinal parasites, leveraging the power of deep learning. We constructed a Deep Belief Network (DBN) utilizing a dataset of 1,000 images sourced from the literature. The results demonstrate that the proposed DBN achieves an outstanding accuracy of 98.8% in categorizing these parasite samples.

This paper introduces a value function to evaluate an investment and reinsurance strategy for two competing insurers, accounting for their combined asset returns and risk exposure. The model operates within a common environment characterized by regime-switching jump-diffusion processes, where the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) partial-integral-differential equation (PIDE) governing the value function proves intractable due to being of first order and non-zero-sum. To address this, the authors convert the first-order HJI PIDE into an equivalent second-order form, which can then be solved using the well-established finite difference method. The findings demonstrate that the optimal approximation error of the value function is second-order with respect to the spatial step size $\Delta x$ and first-order with respect to the temporal step size $\Delta t$. Numerical simulations are provided to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

This study introduces a novel dual-arm cooperative control method designed to enhance the smoothness and stability of flying structures. A primary challenge with dual-arm systems is ensuring the arms move synchronously to prevent the formation of unstable shapes. To address this, we developed a dual-arm simplex algorithm (PIDA) that integrates two distinct phases: a phase-based simplex algorithm (PDSA) and a probabilistic dual-arm simplex algorithm (DPSA). The PDSA ensures the arms remain in a convex configuration, while the DPSA facilitates synchronized arm movement. Furthermore, we implemented a high-precision, low-cost tracking filter based on a hybrid of Kalman filtering and genetic algorithms. This filter combines the superior noise reduction capabilities of Kalman filtering with the robust parameter adaptability of a pre-trained genetic algorithm. The combined PIDA/PIDA and filter system was validated through experiments involving a 1.2 kg quadcopter equipped with two 100 mm arms. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

We present a rigorous and unified framework for analyzing low-energy pion-nucleon interactions, grounded in the simultaneous enforcement of unitarity and analyticity. Our discussion centers on the joint application of these principles to both charged and neutral channels. We derive the isospin amplitudes for charged-pion scattering from the corresponding isospin-1/2 amplitudes for real free nucleons and pions. Furthermore, our approach incorporates dispersion relations alongside unitarity constraints to establish rigorous bounds on the coupling constants of neutral channels. We also provide a comprehensive examination of the dispersion relations for the $s$-wave neutral amplitude, specifically within the so-called $d$-region.

CMS is a general-purpose collider detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHN) designed to analyze proton-proton collisions within the 8-TeV regime. To enhance its capacity for handling higher luminosity data, the detector is undergoing a comprehensive upgrade. This upgrade includes a new pixel detector composed of approximately 7.6 million silicon sensors organized into blades. CMS initially commissioned a pilot detector featuring 162 such optical blades. This paper outlines the progress achieved in CMS Phase-1, detailing the reconstruction of these 162 optical pilot blades.

We present a study of 1,000 active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies with redshifts below 1, selected from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Field Survey. We identify these objects using photometric redshifts and X-ray emission detected via the Chandra and XMM-Ne satellites. By analyzing their visual morphologies, we classify them into three categories: spiral, elliptical, and irregular/irregular-like. Our results indicate that approximately 50% of these AGN reside in spiral galaxies, 25% in elliptical galaxies, and the remaining 25% in irregular galaxies. Additionally, we observe a trend where AGN are more likely to be hosted by spiral galaxies at lower redshifts, but this association weakens as redshift increases.

This study explores various phase-space distributions used to characterize nucleon-nucleus short-range correlations (SRCs). We utilize the Wigner-Wigner (W-W) phase-space representation to construct the phase distribution for nucleons within a nucleus, employing both the Fermi gas and the Fermi sea models. Additionally, we examine nucleon density and the Wigner-Wigner distribution within the Fermi gas framework using the Local Density Approximation method. Our analysis reveals that both the Fermi gas and Fermi sea SRC models are compatible with experimental data. We further demonstrate that the inclusion of finite nuclear density does not significantly alter the phase-space distribution of SRCs. Finally, we assess the impact of SRCs on the nucleon self-energy within the local density approximation, highlighting that the dominant influence is the non-locality of the SRC potential.

This study introduces a comprehensive framework for deriving exact solutions to two fundamental challenges in deep learning: (1) finding a model that fits training data perfectly and (2) constructing a model that separates training examples based on their labels. While prior exact solutions exist primarily for real-valued outputs, this work extends them to the complex plane. By adopting a piecewise constant function architecture, we demonstrate that perfect classification within a complex-valued setting is achievable. Furthermore, we provide specific constructions that satisfy margin conditions, thereby offering a mathematically rigorous justification for the efficacy of complex-output neural networks.

This work examines the saturation of gluon densities within both deep inelastic ep scattering events and nuclear systems. Gaining insight into gluon saturation is essential for elucidating the structure of nuclei and nuclear matter, as well as for modeling the initial stages of heavy ion collisions. We demonstrate that the DGLAP evolution equation inherently limits gluon density through a nonlinear feedback mechanism, causing the gluon distribution function to saturate when the longitudinal momentum fraction $x$ falls below a critical threshold $x_s$. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that both $x_s$ and the saturation gluon density $g_s$ are functions of the transverse momentum $k_t$, exhibiting geometrical scaling. This behavior arises because gluon distributions in confined systems are governed by the gluon density per unit area, a concept grounded in the concept of unitarity. The validity of this geometrical scaling is confirmed by comparing numerical DGLAP calculations with experimental data from the HERA collider.

We investigate the origins of amplitude dispersion in low-metallicity stars by conducting a comprehensive analysis of 1,000 oscillation modes from the Kepler light curve of KIC 8472215. This analysis includes determining the oscillation modes, amplitudes, and frequency separations, followed by a detailed examination of the non-adiabatic driving of oscillation modes. Our findings reveal that the observed amplitude dispersion is primarily caused by magnetic activity, which is further corroborated by the correlation between the observed and predicted rotational periods. Specifically, magnetic activity is shown to affect oscillation modes most significantly when the mode's nodal count is high and the oscillation occurs near the stellar surface. Additionally, our results indicate that magnetic activity influences p-modes more strongly than g-modes.

This paper presents a novel toolbox designed to assess the sensitivity of machine learning (ML) models, which are increasingly vital in financial applications. Our approach applies ML to analyze data from financial literacy tests, with the specific objective of determining how financial knowledge influences investment decisions. Consequently, we offer a methodological framework for researchers to validate their ML findings through sensitivity analysis. Our demonstration utilizes three core techniques: parameter-based analysis to test robustness against hyperparameters, target-based analysis to identify target features driving model performance, and perturbation-based analysis to observe how input data alterations affect outputs.

This study introduces a novel Quantum SQUID M neural Intelligence (QSMI) framework, which merges the capabilities of quantum computing with advanced SQUID M neural networks. The proposed architecture is designed to leverage the precise current and voltage measurements of SQUID M neural networks to facilitate reliable quantum readout. The quantum algorithm developed under this model is capable of performing both single-layer and two-layer classification tasks. The study concludes that the presented QSMI structure offers a significant step toward the practical application of quantum-enhanced machine intelligence.

Warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds are investigated within the framework of almost contact structures, specifically almost contact metric and semi-Riemannian manifolds. The study derives fundamental results concerning the geometry of such submanifolds when embedded in a Heisenberg group or more generally into a hyperplane defined by a constant mean curvature. Finally, the paper presents several illustrative examples to support these theoretical findings.

The PALEOCCENE framework represents a proposed passive, low-energy detector for identifying light, low-energy nuclear recoils. This system utilizes high-purity, high-molecular-weight glass doped with trace amounts of trace metal ions. When exposed to ionizing radiation, trace metal ions in the glass form stable color centers that act as point defects capable of recording the radiation signal. These generated optical defects can be detected via transmission spectroscopy, which measures the optical absorption of the glass.

The approach is entirely passive, meaning it requires no external electric fields or magnetic fields and does not need to be cooled. It is also non-reusable; the glass can only capture radiation events once. The glass can be exposed to ionizing radiation for a period of time, and the signal can be measured at a later date.

This study investigates the behavior of colloidal molecules composed of two active colloids, where inter-particle activity varies. We demonstrate that the system's dynamics are governed by two competing timescales: the time required to traverse a particle's own size and the time needed to move an active particle relative to its dormant partner. This second timescale is sensitive to inter-particle activity levels, enabling the exploration of diverse transport mechanisms. Through active Brownian dynamics simulations, we identify three primary dynamical regimes—translational diffusion, hopping, and tumbling—dictated by inter-particle activity, initial separation, and orientation. Furthermore, we map the steady-state orientation distribution of the particles, observing a transition from a uniform to an anisotropic distribution as activity increases. This anisotropy drives a non-reciprocal interaction between the pair, which, combined with self-interaction, facilitates self-propulsion. Finally, we analyze the transition from a diffusive to a super-diffusive regime by examining both short- and long-time mean squared displacement.

The total spectrum of fractional quantum Hall systems can be effectively described by applying a gauge field to the composite fermion theory of Laughlin. This approach reveals that the magnetic flux experienced by composite fermions is proportional to the system's total spin, a concept previously identified in the context of bilayer systems. This theoretical framework has been expanded to encompass the effects of an external magnetic field and accurately reproduces the energy spectra of the Moore-Read state and the Read-Chiaferotini state. Furthermore, this model predicts the existence of multiple magnetorotons in such systems, a phenomenon previously observed in the non-fractional quantum Hall regime under similar bilayer conditions.

This study examines the spatial characteristics of outbreak clusters within networks, specifically focusing on the fundamental question: given a network and a set of infected nodes, how can we identify the subset of susceptible nodes that are most vulnerable to infection? We introduce a geometric framework where the network is represented as a weighted metric space, and the infection dynamics are modeled through a closed set of points in this space. Our analysis establishes the existence and uniqueness of the optimal infectable set and provides insights into its geometric structure. Additionally, we outline a constructive algorithm capable of identifying this set. The work further explores the asymptotic properties of the optimal set as the total number of susceptible individuals grows infinitely large. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical simulations performed on various synthetic networks and real-world datasets.

This study examines the impact of nearby X sources on CMB map-making processes. We demonstrate that standard maximum likelihood (ML) reconstruction algorithms remain largely unaffected by such sources, even when they are bright. However, when X sources are not properly subtracted, the resulting CMB maps may exhibit residual artifacts. To address this, we propose a straightforward method for identifying X sources using only observational data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and the BICEP2/Keck Array experiments. Our approach involves calculating the maximum likelihood estimates for CMB maps while allowing for point sources at every pixel and then analyzing the resulting map of point-source locations for significant peaks.

"Many AI agents, such as goal-conditioned reinforcement learners, rely on natural language instructions to define their objectives. However, these instructions often contain ambiguous references to objects, requiring a mapping to resolve ambiguity before goals can be established. This paper introduces a method to eliminate such referential ambiguity during the goal definition phase. The process involves using visual attention networks to track entity references within goal definitions, while also employing a semantic network to maintain identity between different mentions of the same entity throughout an episode. The effectiveness of this approach was validated on two tasks: a simulated kitchen domain featuring a single robot and a simulated driving environment populated with multiple entities. Results demonstrate that our method surpasses a baseline model in successfully establishing goals amidst ambiguity."

This work introduces a procedure to characterize a quantum channel utilizing shadow techniques. Our method employs shadow norms to establish upper bounds on various figures of merit for the tomography process. These limits are subsequently converted into concrete tomographic protocols, the efficacy of which is demonstrated through applications to specific channels, including depolarizing and dephasing models. Notably, for the depolarizing channel, the proposed method achieves a sample complexity that is independent of system size. Furthermore, the study explores the potential of these approaches within the context of quantum metrology.

This paper addresses the estimation of the Cheeger constant within convex domains in the Euclidean plane. We establish two sharp inequalities: one relating this constant to the square root of the ratio between perimeter and area, and another connecting it to the square root of the ratio between the square of the perimeter and the moment of inertia. These findings sharpen and extend prior work by J\^ozefiak and by B\^ezdek and Henneberg, respectively. We further demonstrate that, among all convex domains possessing a fixed Cheeger constant, the disk minimizes perimeter while the figure-eight point set maximizes the moment of inertia. Finally, we prove that, for a fixed perimeter, the Cheeger function of any convex domain approaches its limit along a sequence of shapes that converge weakly to a disk.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly recognized as a promising solution for delivering wireless connectivity to hard-to-reach locations. To maximize the utility of this capability, researchers have developed numerous UAV trajectory designs. However, most existing studies prioritize minimizing flight paths to reduce energy usage, often neglecting specific application-driven goals such as maximizing the number of served users within a fixed time window. Addressing this gap, this paper introduces path optimization techniques tailored to enhance service delivery for a time-constrained set of users. The work begins by defining the Maximum Service Users (MSU) problem, an application-specific metric, and demonstrates that it is NP-hard. Subsequently, we propose a sub-optimal algorithm based on a greedy approach to solve MSU. Finally, we evaluate the proposed methods using both analytical and simulation frameworks to validate their performance.

We examine low-energy properties of bilayer graphene within a renormalization group framework, incorporating long-range Coulomb interactions. Our findings indicate that while both intralayer and interlayer couplings remain marginal in non-interacting systems, Coulomb effects drive them relevant, triggering many-body instabilities. Specifically, interlayer interactions acquire velocity-dependent corrections, whereas the functional form of the renormalization group equation for the intrayer coupling mirrors bilayernoninteracting systems. We identify two distinct instability scenarios: charge density wave ordering at commensurate wavevectors, and superconductivity. The latter is particularly notable as it arises from interlayer scattering channels, offering a fresh perspective on superconductivity in graphene-based materials.

The endohedral fullerenes, exemplified by Sc2TbN@C80, represent a compelling class of materials for spintronics and magnetic resonance imaging. This study utilizes scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy to examine the temperature-dependent conformational switching of Sc2TbTbN@C80, revealing a distinct critical temperature (Tc) of 100 K. Above this threshold, the isomers adopt a D5h symmetry, whereas below it, the configuration shifts to D5. This structural transition is attributed to the diamagnetic state of the Tb ion at temperatures exceeding Tc, resulting in Tc = 100 K. Furthermore, spectroscopic data indicate that the energy separation between f-orbital levels in Tb3+ diminishes as temperature rises, a finding that corroborates the observed morphological changes.

To mitigate these risks, it is essential to employ robust encryption algorithms capable of compactly securing data transmission. This paper introduces a new encryption technique designed specifically for the low-powered IoT sector. Our approach leverages the discrete logarithm problem alongside modular exponentiation, utilizing a shared prime number and a primitive root as the foundational keys for the two parties. This study introduces a sequential Bayesian experimental design that optimizes the overall precision of parameter estimation within a series of Ramsey measurements. We demonstrate the superiority of this adaptive approach over both the global optimal strategy and the standard non-adaptive method, in which individual measurements are executed without prior knowledge of previous outcomes. The results are particularly significant for systems characterized by long dephasing times, where adaptive optimization yields a substantial enhancement in estimation fidelity.

We introduce a novel network centrality metric, Gromov Centrality (GOC), rooted in metric geometry. GOC leverages the triangle inequality excess to quantify the fundamental distances between all node pairs, offering a comprehensive view of a network's multi-scale architecture. This approach effectively captures both the global and localized structural characteristics of complex systems. We demonstrate that the GOC algorithm is computationally efficient, capable of processing massive datasets like Wikipedia and citation graphs within a few seconds, and even manages to analyze the entire structure of the human brain's connectome. Our analysis reveals that GOC provides a more accurate assessment of node importance in biological contexts, particularly highlighting the critical roles of hub neurons. Furthermore, we find that this new metric exhibits significantly lower noise levels compared to traditional centrality measures, thereby enhancing its reliability for analyzing neural connectivity.

This work introduces a new gravitational framework that extends the principles of General Relativity and Newtonian gravity. By utilizing a new tensor and scalar field, the model maintains relativistic field equations consistent with the original theory but introduces specific modifications. While retaining relativistic invariance, the model breaks both spatial and azimuthal symmetry. A key innovation involves a new scalar field that alters gravitational interactions based on the direction of the source, a factor absent in General Relativity and Newtonian gravity. Consequently, the model predicts that the gravitational force exerted by a spherical mass is not uniform in all directions. This directional dependence is demonstrated through calculations showing that the gravitational field of a sphere varies with the polar angle, a result derived from the modified field equations.

This study focuses on bundles of matrix operators with complex-valued operator coefficients that vary over $\mathbb{C}^{m}$, which are classified into four types: $m$th-degree monic, general, $m$th-degree non-unitary, and linear bundles. We determine the invariants of these specific bundle types and establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for the convergence of any two such bundles. The paper also addresses the classification problem for each of these four categories. Additionally, it provides an overview of the fundamental properties inherent in operator bundles.

The treewidth of a graph is a fundamental parameter that approximates graph treeness, and its importance is highlighted by the Strong Exclusion Graph Theorem, which asserts that minor-free graphs with bounded excluded minors have bounded treewidth. While this result is known to hold for large radius, it has a more complex status for graphs with small radii. We present a positive finding for such metrics: we demonstrate that both planar graphs and a broader category of weakly minor-free graphs possess treewidth representations with low and bounded values. Our findings are made possible by introducing a new algorithm to construct low treewidth decompositions for large-radius planar graphs. This approach leverages the Bounded-Radius Exclusion Principle, which establishes that large-radius planar graphs possess bounded-radius minor subgraphs. We further extend this method to weakly minor-free graphs by applying a similar bounded-radius exclusion theorem. Additionally, our paper presents a novel proof of the Strong Exclusion Graph Theorem for minor-free graphs and provides an alternative proof of Bodlaender and Koster's theorem regarding the bounded treewidth of large-radius graphs with fixed genus.

This study establishes that for strongly monotonic, smooth discrete-time dynamical systems featuring a compact, convex domain with boundary repulsion, prevalent trajectories exhibit asymptotic convergence to the unique globally stable fixed point. The demonstrated proof relies on an assumption of compact, convex positivity, wherein the system decomposes into independent lower-dimensional subsystems. The findings are generalized to include discrete-time systems that are only continuously differentiable, incorporating a theorem that ensures the convergence of the second variation along the global attractor to the zero operator. These results are further extended to cover the asymptotic convergence to a unique globally stable periodic orbit.

Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE) are widely used for determining the ground state of quantum systems, yet their application remains constrained by the exponential scaling of circuit depth tied to the number of qubits. This study introduces "Qubit-excitation-based VQE" (QE-VQE), an adaptive framework that reduces circuit depth by linking the number of qubits to the excitation count of the ground state rather than the total qubit count. This approach is demonstrated in two contexts: first, using a classical gate-based model for the nitrogen impurity in a diamond lattice, where the qubit count scales with the system's electronic excitations; second, employing an effective spin-1/2 model for two-dimensional cuprate superconductors, where qubit usage scales with hole-doping levels. In both cases, QE-VQE offers a more efficient alternative to QMC and standard VQE methods.

Deep generative models, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), are typically employed to learn latent variable distributions from data, with their variational parameters derived using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) to maximize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). In contrast, this work demonstrates that maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation is also effective for obtaining generative model parameters and represents the ELBO's direct maximization. We further show that applying this approach to variational parameters yields closed-form solutions for the encoder. Consequently, this "closed-form VAE" eliminates the need for encoder training, streamlining the process to require only the maximization of the ELBO via an SGD-based optimization for the generative model components. Empirical results indicate that this method not only accelerates training but also enhances the quality of both learned latent space representations and generated data.

The detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) is anticipated to offer a transformative window into the early universe. This study examines SGWB detection prospects by combining projected sensitivities from space- and ground-based interferometers with cosmological models. We utilize a framework where the SGWB arises from a power-law spectrum amplified by a period of accelerated expansion following inflation. In this scenario, the spectral tilt and amplitude of the observable SGWB are governed by the dynamics of the early universe and the equation of state of the acceleration phase. We assess detectability across three scenarios: a SGWB emerging directly from inflation, one amplified during reheating, and one generated later and amplified later. Our findings indicate that an SGWB originating from inflation or reheating is unlikely to be identified by current or near-future detectors, whereas an amplified SGWB from a later epoch could be observed by next-generation interferometers. Additionally, we explore the SGWB's impact on the Hubble tension, concluding that while an SGWB alone cannot resolve the discrepancy, it could alleviate the tension when combined with other physics beyond the standard model.

We report the inaugural spectral survey of Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) utilizing the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). This study targets the $J=1-0$ rotational transition of carbon monosulfide (CS) at 4.21 GHz, a molecule that is difficult to observe with a single-element antenna due to its low frequency. Our observations, conducted with the 12-m receiver of the ACA, detected CS emission from the comet with a peak flux density of 0.045 mJy, situated 0.15° from the nucleus. We confirm that this emission is not local contamination from the Sun or the Milky Way by analyzing spectral line features and by cross-checking against reference spectra from the aforementioned sources. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the detected signal originates from a dispersed distribution of CS rather than a concentrated source within the coma. This finding supports the hypothesis that cometary outgassing can generate molecular line emission detectable by high-resolution interferometers even when the emitting molecules are not densely concentrated near the nucleus.

This study presents an unsupervised speech synthesis framework that universalizes speaker-dependent neural speech generation, requiring neither speaker-specific data nor external language resources. By leveraging available text-to-speech models, we introduce a novel technique to enhance unsupervised auto-tuning for speaker adaptation. Our approach demonstrates that meaningful speech outputs can be created without any labeled audio from the target speaker. Furthermore, we evaluate our unsupervised adaptation technique on a large dataset, showing that our synthesized voices achieve superior naturalness and similarity to the target speaker compared to conventional self-supervised adaptation methods.

This study investigates a quintessence framework where the energy density of the universe is described by a complex number and the scale factor is governed by a Tsallis holographic dark energy (HDE) model. We demonstrate that when the quintessence potential is expressed in terms of the scale factor, the resulting Tsallis HDE takes a quintessence-like form. Furthermore, we establish that the derived Lagrangian for Tsallis HDE is identical to the Lagrangian of the complex number quintessence field. Finally, we analyze the cosmological dynamics of this complex number quintessence system.

This study introduces a branch-and-bound framework enhanced with NSGA-II to tackle the solution of multi-objective mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problems. The proposed strategy leverages the strength of the NSGA-II algorithm, a well-established multi-objective evolutionary method known for generating diverse and high-quality solutions. By integrating this heuristic approach within a rigorous branch-and-bound structure, the method offers a robust framework applicable to various real-world scenarios. To validate its efficacy, the authors applied the method to a novel line sizing problem in a power distribution network, which involves multiple objectives and multiple local optima. The results demonstrate that the enhanced branch-and-bound NSGA-II approach successfully identifies the complete set of Pareto optimal solutions.

This work demonstrates within the framework of Smooth Infinitesimal Dialectics (SDD) that internal Lie groupoids in cartesian closed differential categories (cCDDs) are integral complete and internally linked. Specifically, we establish that an internal Lie groupoid possesses integral complete representations precisely when its internal Lie algebra is integral complete, with this completeness occurring if and only if the groupoid is linked internally. These findings extend previous work by Jacobs and van Oostrom, who addressed internal Lie groups in the same setting.

The rapid advancement of data-driven research in biology and medicine is driven by the increasing volume of data generated and the growing necessity for complex computational analyses. While data sharing is vital for scientific progress, it faces significant hurdles, particularly within the biomedical field, due to concerns regarding intellectual property, security, privacy, and data sovereignty. To address these challenges, we introduce a secure sharing framework designed specifically for complex biomedical analyses. This approach leverages modern cloud computing capabilities and incorporates advanced techniques such as data encryption, federated analysis models, and the utilization of trusted cyberinfrastructure gateways. We have developed a flexible framework that enables the secure sharing of complex datasets between researchers and computational resources, allowing for processing without transferring the actual data. To validate this method, we implemented a framework based on the DataONE global data infrastructure, which features trusted gateways at three major sites: the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the National Cancer Institute (NCI), and the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI). This configuration allows data providers to upload information securely to a gateway, where authorized users can access it for analysis on local infrastructure, all while the data never leaves its original location.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine emotional sentiments toward specific components within an issue, such as distinct attributes in product reviews. While existing models for ABSP typically rely on either task-specific fine-tuning or pre-training on vast, unlabelled corpora, they often fail to explicitly capture the implicit sentiment inherent within text. To address this, we introduce a new framework called iEmo, which integrates Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (iEmo) with an emotion-implicit architecture. Specifically, iEmo leverages the robust representational capabilities of Sup-CoP (Supervised Contrastive Pre-training) to enhance sentiment feature extraction. Furthermore, we developed an emotion-implicit architecture designed to simultaneously identify explicit sentiments associated with specific aspects and implicit sentiments present in reviews. Experimental results across two standard ABSP data sets indicate that iEmo achieves performance comparable to or superior to current state-of-the-art methods.

We establish the identification conditions for direct and indirect effects associated with binary mediators in the context of the 2-stage 1-time model, specifically when data are gathered via case-control sampling. Our findings demonstrate that, provided specific assumptions hold, this sampling strategy remains a valid approach for estimating the overall effect of an intervention. Furthermore, we outline assumptions necessary to ensure the identifiability of a subset of mediational pathways. Finally, leveraging assumptions regarding the absence of confounding, we propose an estimator for direct and indirect effects that does not require knowledge of the sampling probabilities.

This study investigates secure multi-user communication networks enhanced by Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS), accounting for hardware impairments. The objective is to minimize the overall secrecy outage probability (SOP) by optimizing passive beamforming matrices for the RSI. Since acquiring full knowledge of channel state information (CSI) is impractical, this paper focuses on robust beamforming strategies that function under uncertainties. To achieve this, we integrate the random vector Fading (RVF) model with a unified framework encompassing amplitude and phase loading impairments. The resulting beamforming optimization problem is non-convex; therefore, we transform it into an equivalent, more tractable form. The solution approach involves alternating between optimizing the passive beforming matrix and handling the constraints related to passive unit modulus constraints. To address these specific sub-problems, we employ the S-procedure, followed by the application of the Sequential Convex Approximation (SCA) method. Furthermore, we derive an efficient, low-complexity baseline solution for comparison. Finally, we provide numerical results that demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over the simple baseline in terms of SOP performance.

This study introduces a novel reinforcement learning framework termed "Contrastive Value Function Resampling and Augmentation via Hindsight Summarization" (CVFRA-HS). Designed to overcome the limitations of current deep RL methods that rely on fixed, static experience replay buffers, our approach dynamically adjusts the training distribution. By leveraging a buffer of past experiences, we can dynamically generate and augment new experience samples. This augmentation process involves utilizing a policy network to generate trajectories and applying a hindsight summarization agent to assign meaningful reward signals to these new samples. This agent functions by comparing a trajectory's performance against others within the buffer to determine its value. Furthermore, we have developed a specific variant of the contrastive value function that utilizes the cosine similarity of the underlying features to calculate these contrastive scores. This approach effectively stabilizes the learning process and significantly improves the agent's overall performance.

The solar wind originates from the Sun's upper atmosphere, and understanding its genesis is essential for space weather forecasting. While the solar wind's macroscopic properties have been extensively studied, the solar origin of its energy flux remains a critical gap. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission offers unprecedented access to the inner heliosphere, enabling the first direct measurements of solar wind energy flux near the Sun. This paper presents the inaugural analysis of solar breeze energy flux data collected by PSP. We detail the temporal evolution of this energy flux as the probe's perihelion distance decreases and show that it aligns with theoretical models, thereby providing definitive evidence that the solar wind's energy is ultimately derived from the Sun.

We offer a noncommutative generalization of topological principal bundles where the structure group acts noncompactly on $C^*$-algebras, specifically focusing on cases involving countable (not necessarily finite) groups. For these objects, we define their $C^*$-algebra of global sections as the fixed point subalgebra resulting from a specific action on the multilinear or $n$-dimensional (in this case, row and column) tensor product of the underlying algebra. We demonstrate that under these conditions, the relevant action is properly ergodic. Furthermore, we establish several significant topological and geometric properties in this noncommutative framework, including the existence of a local approximate section system, local approximate amenability of the $C^*$-algebra, and a local version of the partition condition.

We establish that it is consistent with ZFC that $\mathcal{P}$ is strictly less than $\mathcal{B}$, while also proving that $\mathcal{B}$ is regular. Additionally, we demonstrate that $\mathcal{B}$ is always strictly less than the continuum, and that $\mathcal{P}$ is less than the continuum. We further characterize the continuum as the supremum of the $\mathcal{P}$-sizes of certain filters, and prove that $\mathcal{B}$ corresponds to the supremum of the $\mathcal{P}$-sizes of certain ultrafilters. This study explores slow and fast light propagation within a $q$-deformed optomechanical setup featuring an inverted steady-state mean photon number in the microwave cavity. Utilizing the weak-field approximation, we derive the dispersion relation to examine how q-deformation and the inversion of the microwave cavity affect group velocities. Our results indicate that achieving multiple group velocities requires both conditions: the presence of $q$-deformation and the inversion of the microwave cavity's steady state. Additionally, we analyze how the $q$-parameter and other system parameters influence the clarity and magnitude of these slow and fast light phenomena.

We employ a model that incorporates the exchange of angular momentum between two rotational components, representing the relative motion of quarks and gluons within a hadron. By analyzing the interaction between these two rotational components, we investigate how an adverse R-parity scissors process affects the hadron's structure. We also examine how angular momentum exchange between these two rotational components influences the hadron's properties. This study introduces a cell-mean based neural network method to address both hyperbolic and parabolic classes of partial differential equations. The approach relies on specific definitions of cell-mean values for unknown functions and their derivatives, which are computed across each control volume of a neural network-informed finite volume framework. Initially, these cell-mean quantities are substituted into a finite volume scheme to generate discrete equations. Subsequently, a neural network constructs continuous representations of these discrete solutions, utilizing the cell-mean data and its gradients as inputs for a continuous neural network architecture. A key advantage of this technique is that the resulting method yields both finite volume-based and neural network-based solutions for the equation being solved. Furthermore, the continuous solution derived via this cell-mean strategy serves as the foundation for a new cell-centered finite element method. The efficacy of this cell-centered approach is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments.

The ALICE experiment is designed to investigate the characteristics of the hot, dense, and strongly-interacting hadronic matter generated by heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To achieve this, the facility employs a sophisticated array of detectors tailored to identify various particle species and analyze their collective behaviors. This comprehensive setup is currently being upgraded to enhance its capabilities for data collection beyond LHC Run 3 and into the High-Luminosity LHC era. This article outlines the proposed enhancements to the detector array, emphasizing improvements in both performance and operational efficiency.

We investigate the relationship between the timelike version of the Unruh effect and Berry phases generated by an observer undergoing uniform acceleration within a spacetime featuring a timelike dimension. This phenomenon arises when an observer's worldline encircles a closed timelike curve (CTC), which can be interpreted as the chromatic aberration (or color shift) of that color. This relationship suggests a new method for experimentally simulating timelike effects using quantum systems capable of exhibiting CTCs.

Disaster response relies heavily on quickly identifying and processing critical information from social media. While numerous studies address disaster response, most concentrate on single languages, leaving the challenge of handling multiple languages largely unexplored. This paper introduces the Multilingual Incident Extraction (MEE) dataset, which was developed to investigate cross-lingual incident detection. Constructed from over 100,000 tweets gathered from 10 distinct disaster events across 6 different languages, the MEE dataset is utilized to train and evaluate a cross-lingual model for incident detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves an F1 score of 0.800, outperforming baseline methods by 0.100 points.

This study investigates the stellar breeze from the companion star in the high-mass black hole binary Cyg X-1, specifically analyzing its impact on X-ray variability and spectra during the hard state. We examined archival data from the Chandra satellite, which offers superior temporal resolution and spectral coverage. Our findings indicate that while the black hole's intrinsic hard X-ray spectrum remains largely unaffected by the stellar wind, the companion's X-ray emission significantly modulates the observed variability at low energies.

This work investigates a non-local action featuring a new vector-type term named the non-abelian ether-like term. Its purpose is to construct a local alternative to the Schwinger-Thomas formalism, a model renowned for describing the vacuum's role as a dark energy component. Unlike the non-abelian Proca theory, a similar local framework, this ether-like term preserves gauge invariance, thereby enabling a future extension to non-abelian Yang-Mills theories. By applying a non-local approach, researchers can rigorously analyze the cosmological implications of a vacuum acting as dark energy, particularly when investigating the theory at finite temperature. Specifically, the study demonstrates that the ether-like term remains gauge-invariant in thermal environments and yields a massive vector boson spectrum.

We propose a joint modeling approach that simultaneously handles syntactic and semantic parsing. Our model is built upon a syntax tree where nodes are annotated with both universal syntactic tags and detailed role labels representing the meaning relations between those roles and their heads. This model allows for efficient generation of both syntax and meaning structures from raw text. We demonstrate that this approach yields significant performance gains in state-of-the-art semantic parsing results, while also producing high-quality syntax trees. This quality of output exceeds previous methods by a wide margin, matching the accuracy of leading parsers for universal dependency parsing.

We investigate magnetized, neutrino-cooled disk outflows following the merger of compact objects, utilizing 2D and 3D general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations. Our results indicate that the jets' magnetization levels are contingent on the specific ratio of magnetic flux to accretion rate. We explore the implications of these findings for the observed afterglows of short gamma-ray bursts.

Tidal features (TFs) are a primary indicator of galaxy mergers and interactions, yet their physical properties and prevalence across different environments remain poorly understood. We present a comprehensive analysis of TFs around 1.1 million early-type galaxies (ETGs) within the 150 square degree patch of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). These features were identified using a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on simulated Tidal Features (TFs) and real ETGs from the MaNGA survey. Our results reveal that the median flux fraction of TFs is 0.001, with a median redshift of 0.25. The feature fraction peaks at approximately 0.04 for objects with stellar masses exceeding $10^{11} M_{\odot}$, a trend that persists up to the highest stellar masses observed ($\sim 10^{12.5} M_{\odot}$). Furthermore, TF density increases with redshift, reaching a maximum of roughly 0.02 at $z=0.5$ before declining.
