Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, intense millisecond-long radio signals of extragalactic origin. While the origins of these bursts remain uncertain, leading theories suggest they arise from interactions involving compact objects such as neutron stars or black holes. We report the discovery of a new FRB, designated FRB 200428, which exhibits a high peak flux of 1.1 Jy and a short duration of 0.8 ms. We conducted simultaneous and delayed optical follow-up observations using the 1.2-meter GTC telescope at the Calar Alto Observatory. Despite extensive searches, no optical counterparts were detected, leading us to establish 3$\sigma$ upper limits on the optical fluence of 0.015 ergs/sq cm and the peak flux density of 0.015 mJy. These limits indicate that FRB 200428 lacks detectable optical emission. Furthermore, we conducted a systematic review of prior optical searches for FRB 200428, which further confirmed the absence of simultaneous or delayed optical signals. Our results align with the hypothesis that the origins of FRBs lie in the accretion disks of supermassive black holes, or they constrain the disk's opacity and the bursts' emission region to be at a distance of no less than 0.0000000000000000000000

This work details the development, improvement, and analysis of two high-energy laser architectures: the Z and Omega linear particle accelerators. We describe a new approach for modeling the time- and space-varying laser pulse shape, utilizing an energy-dependent model that accounts for the frequency variation of absorption. This refined model was applied to optimize the configuration of the laser system at the Z facility, enabling it to generate a peak power of 25 TW. Furthermore, we have created a reverse-engineering methodology to infer the physical characteristics of the laser system based on the observed temporal and spatial evolution of the target's vapor channel.

It is widely recognized that large language models excel at text generation, yet it remains an open question whether they can perform visual tasks. This study investigates the feasibility of integrating visual controls into text generation processes. Our approach involves introducing the visual input alongside the desired output within the model's training data. Experiments conducted on various visual observation tasks demonstrate that even without explicit architectural modifications, pre-trained language models are capable of performing these visual-oriented tasks. Consequently, our findings suggest that current language models possess the potential to observe the world when guided by appropriate fine-tuning.

This research introduces a modified version of the RingCT algorithm to accelerate the completion of Monero transactions. We achieve this by utilizing an optimized ConstantTime library and streamlining the signature process through the delegation of work to more powerful external servers. Additionally, we have created a web-based demonstration that allows users to test the performance improvements of this enhanced algorithm.

This study details the development of a rapid scan technique for measuring the brightness of particle beams. The method involves detecting a fixed-position downstream screen's response to beam intensity variations caused by closed-orbit excursions during optical transport. The resulting scan signal is a complex function of brightness distributions at both upstream and downstream planes, as well as the beamsline geometry connecting them. The paper presents an analytical model for this convolved relationship and outlines a methodology to deconvolute it for brightness distribution recovery. The scan approach is demonstrated using proton beam data from the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and provides a new rapid diagnostic tool for particle beams. The method offers significant potential for brightness distribution optimization and is applicable to various beam types, including those with diffuse or multi-component characteristics.

We introduce a collaborative framework for constructing data-driven reduced-order models of complex systems, leveraging machine learning to optimize the training of individual models. We demonstrate this approach using a data set from a high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics simulation of a high-pressure gas turbine combustor. In this example, we partition the data by pressure levels to develop dynamic models specific to each. Through collaboration, these individual models are combined into a single, robust model that generalizes across the entire pressure range. This methodology is applicable to scenarios where comprehensive data is fragmented into subsets, such as when data collection occurs in isolated time periods or by distinct research groups.

This study examines the decays of $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ (where $n=1,2,3$) via a hadronic loop mechanism. By employing the $Q^4$ power counting rule within the framework of hadronic loops, we determine the relative branching fractions for these processes. The calculated results indicate that the ratios follow the sequence $\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^+)>\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^+)>\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^+)$. This theoretical prediction is consistent with experimental data obtained from the BESIII collaboration.

Training neural networks with quantized weights and targets offers a viable path to deploying models on resource-constrained edge devices. This paper introduces a novel technique that integrates target annealing with constraints to limit quantization errors during the training process. We provide a theoretical justification for the convergence of this approach and demonstrate through experiments on image classification that annealed projective gradient descent successfully reduces quantization error while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Soft robotics represents a rapidly evolving field with growing interest in the development of efficient, precise, and adaptable control strategies. However, achieving modeling that is both accurate and computationally tractable remains a significant hurdle. This paper presents a survey of current soft robot simulation and control approaches, categorizing existing methods into three distinct groups based on their underlying paradigms. The survey also examines various control techniques, including supervised and unsupervised learning, control theory, and energy-based methods, highlighting their respective advantages and limitations. Finally, the authors outline future research directions and potential strategies for overcoming these challenges.

This study addresses the challenge of table-based factual assessment. We introduce a strategy that decomposes tables into individual rows and columns to facilitate the evaluation of specific claims. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this decomposition-based framework surpasses current leading methodologies. Additionally, we release a novel dataset comprising over 11,000 manually crafted questions and answers.

Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) are widely recognized for their ability to generate high-quality samples across diverse fields, yet they typically struggle to address an excessive number of conditions. This paper introduces a novel architecture that incorporates a learnable representation of conditions within a latent space, enabling the model to capture shared patterns among numerous conditions and thereby expanding cGAN capabilities. Our approach is validated using a synthetic dataset featuring numerous parameter configurations, demonstrating that the proposed method successfully generates diverse and realistic samples.

Bayesian nested sampling (BNS) serves as a robust technique for simultaneous posterior inference and model comparison, though its computational intensity restricts application to scenarios where the posterior distribution is non-trivial to compute. A recent advancement, Step Nested Sampling (SNP), significantly accelerates the process by integrating stepwise sampling to conduct post-processing on results from the original BNS. This study evaluates various sampling strategies used within SNPs by comparing their performance across two specific examples. Our findings indicate that the most diverse sampling steps—specifically those utilizing Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)—consistently outperform other methods in terms of posterior estimation accuracy and the precision of Bayesian model comparison metrics. Additionally, the quantity of distinct sampling steps employed during the SNPs phase is a critical determinant of the algorithm's overall efficiency.

We introduce an $(O(n), 1)$-error distance labeling scheme tailored for planar graphs that withstand the failure of up to $k = O(\sqrt{n})$ vertices. For any set of up to $k$ failed vertices and any path segment within the graph, the labels of the path's start and end points suffice to determine the distance between them, assuming the labels along the connecting route within the failed section are unavailable. This capability extends to scenarios where up to $k$ edges are instead treated as failed. Our construction relies on an auxiliary $(O(n), 1)$-error fault-resilient labeling scheme for the entire graph; the scheme determines the distance to a specific target vertex with a maximum multiplicative error of at most 1.5. Additionally, we present an algorithm that constructs such labeling schemes for general graphs with a bit complexity of $O(n^{2.5})$ and a runtime of $O(n^{2.5})$.

We investigate time-domain two-particle correlations within a forced dissipative Bose-Hubbub model by analyzing both second-order correlation functions and joint detection probabilities. Our analysis demonstrates that the temporal signature of these correlations is governed by distinct probabilities of particle arrival sequences, which in turn depend on the underlying quantum state of the system. Specifically, we find that joint detection probabilities are dictated by the probabilities of finding $N$ particles in their respective initial positions, thereby encoding the initial state's probability distribution. Consequently, these correlations offer a new perspective on how quantum interference and state engineering intersect in dissipative processes.

This work establishes C¹ theory for divergence-form elliptic equations with $L^2$ coefficients that are interpreted as $L^2$-currents. It demonstrates that $L^2$-currents are the most natural class of $L^2$-based objects that maintain stability under weak convergence and subsequence extraction. Furthermore, we construct a counter-example illustrating that such a theoretical framework cannot be developed for $L^1$ functions in a divergence form. Additionally, we present a concise counter-example to a C¹-regularity claim for the divergence of a vector field in $L^2$, thereby supporting a recently discovered negative result by J. C. Sogge.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of using statistical strata for identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, particularly in the context of Gaussian processes (GP). However, this approach has two significant limitations: it treats all data points as belonging to a single distribution and lacks a method for learning the parameters of these strata. To address these issues, we introduce a novel model that employs distributional Gaussian processes (DGPs) to characterize multiple data strata. This framework enables the identification of potential OOD samples and was tested on synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our model outperforms standard GP-based distributional frameworks and existing OOD detection techniques.

This finding represents an advancement over the findings of [10]. Additionally, we derive uniform Hölder continuity for the gradient of the equation's solution.

This study addresses the challenge of real-time Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and networking Service Function Chaining (SFC) within fog environments, specifically focusing on the dynamic nature of SFC service flows. To achieve this, we propose a novel framework that integrates fault prediction, joint failure restoration and energy efficiency, and flow scheduling. The fault prediction mechanism utilizes an online learning approach to dynamically estimate failure probabilities, while flow scheduling and resource management jointly optimize service flow performance and resource consumption. The proposed flow scheduling strategy ensures that SFC service flows are resilient against disruptions, energy-efficient, and meet Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through extensive simulations comparing it against several existing methods.

Gradient surgery serves as an effective diagnostic technique for evaluating how individual loss components influence training dynamics and final model performance. By analyzing a diverse range of parameterizations and hyperparameters, this study reveals that conventional loss function selection methods are often insufficient. Furthermore, the authors introduce a generalizable framework for designing loss functions, which can be applied to various tasks and problems.

This study examines the population of filaments in the Galactic Center region, specifically analyzing the spacing between them. Utilizing data from the Herschel Space Observatory, we identified filaments within a 300 pc radius of the Sun, utilizing a minimum width threshold of 3 light-years. The analysis reveals that the distribution of inter-filament distances is non-Gaussian and is best modeled by a power-law distribution. Additionally, the average separation between filaments is found to be 1.4 pc, a scale that is consistent with the typical spacing of molecular clouds in this area. These results suggest that filaments are embedded within larger, pre-existing molecular cloud structures.

The rising integration of distributed generation (DG) and electric vehicles (EVs) has intensified voltage violations within distribution networks. Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) is a cost-effective primary control strategy that mitigates these issues by lowering bus voltages. However, in modern distributed energy resource environments, traditional, centralized CVR approaches face significant limitations. This paper introduces a novel, fully decentralized algorithm to execute optimal conservation voltage reduction. Leveraging the gossip method, this distributed approach enables primary controllers across all buses to autonomously determine ideal setpoints without reliance on centralized coordination. The proposed solution is validated through simulations on the 123-bus IEEE test system under various scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness.

This study investigates nonstochastic bandit scenarios augmented by arm-specific delays, where choosing an inferior arm incurs a time-dependent cost. We introduce a framework involving both bandits and external advisors, requiring us to balance exploration against delay-induced costs while respecting the constraint that selecting an arm with a current active delay period is forbidden. We demonstrate that in pure nonstochastic settings, a complete absence of prior knowledge about delay structures renders the task impossible to approach within constant multiplicative factors of the optimal. However, we show that incorporating limited prior information regarding delay patterns allows for sublinear regret relative to the optimal. We also prove that for specific, simplified delay models, optimal performance can be achieved through simple greedy strategies. Extending our analysis to the combined problem of bandits and advisors, we establish that the optimal arm selection becomes feasible in a broader class of delay models featuring latency induced by both external advisors and inherent delays from bandit decisions.

We introduce LEATHER, a new approach to generating human-like conversational text. Our framework is designed to create dialogue that mimics human production processes by leveraging a latent space to filter and refine initial drafts, thereby enhancing both diversity and coherence. We demonstrate that LEATHER significantly surpasses current state-of-the-line methods on standard evaluation benchmarks. Additionally, we present two new datasets, LEATHER-1 and LEATHER-2, constructed using our model to support future research.

This study examines the behavior of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) under finite temperature and chemical potential, with a particular focus on the quark-gluon plasma and the evolution of hadronic matter as it crosses the phase transition to QCD. The discussion begins by outlining the theoretical framework and numerical techniques employed in lattice QCD, followed by an exploration of the hadronic sector at low $T$ and $\mu$, specifically analyzing chiral dynamics, meson properties, and baryon currents. The narrative then shifts to the quark-gluon plasma regime at high $T$ and $\mu$, covering aspects such as the equation of state, Debye screening, jet quenching parameters, and transport coefficients. The concluding section investigates the nature of the phase transition separating these two states across varying thermodynamic conditions, highlighting the critical point and the boundaries of the hadronic bag within the phase diagram.

This paper introduces a probabilistic surrogate model designed to estimate offshore wind turbine loads, utilizing chained Gaussian processes to navigate the complex, multi-stage load transmission chain. This framework effectively captures stress correlations across different structural locations and uncertainties arising from environmental variables. Validated against 15 months of measured data from the Hywind Scotland array, the model achieves significant computational efficiency compared to standard time-domain simulations while maintaining a high degree of accuracy.

Natural disasters can be anticipated, mitigated, and managed more effectively by analyzing social media. This study examines how Twitter users responded to the earthquake that struck Izmir on October 30, 2020. The analysis, which covers tweets from October 30 to November 1, 2020, involves a dataset of 1.1 million messages. We identified and analyzed 100,000 of these to determine the specific impact of the outage. Our findings indicate that the affected tweets were 100 times less frequent than those unrelated to the disaster, and that the content was 100 percent Turkish.

We introduce a forward-optimization approach for inverse problems, specifically designed to reconstruct the initial conditions of a time-evolving system from data collected at a later time. This method relies on representing both the forward solution and its derivative with respect to the initial state using reduced spaces constructed via the proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of high-fidelity simulations. These POD modes are generated by solving the normal equations associated with the adjoint equation. We establish that this strategy offers a data-dependent, stability-controlled solution and demonstrate its robustness against data noise. Furthermore, we apply this framework to inverse problems within nonlinear partial differential equations, confirming its effectiveness through numerical experiments on the Burgers and Navier-Stokes equations.

This paper introduces SceNDD, a naturalistic driving dataset featuring 100 hours of footage collected from 5 vehicles. Annotators have marked 100,000 scenarios, each tagged with functional driver states, vehicle dynamics, and environmental factors. Annotating these scenarios required a custom system incorporating both a video playback interface and synchronized data annotation tools. The factorization of scenarios into modular sub-factors allows for precise modeling of situational dynamics and supports the rigorous validation of automated techniques. The dataset and its annotation tools are available at https://github.com/ITCAResearch/SceNDD.

Boundary and interface conformal field theories (ICFTs) are characterized by their structure of two-dimensional conformal blocks that alternate between the bulk theory and its boundary counterpart. In this study, we introduce a specific interface model consisting of a bulk theory coupled with an identical boundary theory. We demonstrate that the boundary entropy of such a system can be expressed as the sum of the entropies of mixed boundary operators, which are identified as reflections of the bulk spectrum. This relationship is validated using explicit computations in a $G$-twisted WZW framework paired with its boundary version, where the bulk theory is based on the group $G$ and the boundary is its identity sector. Furthermore, the boundary entropy of this system is numerically equivalent to the boundary entropy of the twisted bulk WZW theory itself.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a promising technology to overcome the limitations of radio environments and boost 5G/6G wireless systems. This study investigates channel estimation in RIS-assisted orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) systems, specifically addressing circular prefix (CP) truncation and imperfections in both transceiver and RIS hardware. A new circularly truncated channel matrix model is developed to represent these real-world constraints. To mitigate these challenges, a reduced-complexity enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM) is proposed for channel estimation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms conventional compressed sensing-based methods and standard ELM in terms of accuracy while offering superior computational efficiency.

The Energy-Integral Variation (EIV) theorem, which establishes the necessity of energy measurements across all complete sets of eigenstates for the energy operator, has been challenged by a counter-example. This critique questions the feasibility of measuring an energy eigenstate with a discrete non-degenerate spectrum that relies on isolated systems and assumes measurement processes must be ideal. This analysis argues that both the theoretical framework of that counter-example and its underlying assumptions are fundamentally flawed. It is demonstrated that even in scenarios involving infinite degeneracy or arbitrarily high precision, complete energy measurement via a single quantum energy interaction remains theoretically possible. This conclusion holds true whether utilizing projective or non-projective measurement formalisms, provided the measurement setup involves an auxiliary system. This capability validates the EIV theorem's correctness and simultaneously underscores the energy measurement completeness required by the theorem for both scenarios involving isolated and non-isolated quantum systems.

The widespread adoption of contact tracing applications has become a crucial element in combating the COVID-19 pandemic. These apps facilitate the digital monitoring of individuals who may have been exposed to the virus by enabling users to anonymously share their location data and health status. While this approach offers significant potential, it also raises substantial privacy concerns regarding personal information protection. This study introduces a specific class of probabilistic logic programming problems termed "prob-stp," which encompasses a unique subclass known as "Coronavirus-SUS." These models reflect the privacy risks faced by individuals and can be effectively analyzed using established privacy metrics such as $\epsilon$-differential privacy and differential privacy. By applying an $\epsilon$-differential privacy framework to Coronavirus-SUS instances, we demonstrate that both location data and health data can be securely shared while maintaining privacy guarantees. Furthermore, we present a novel stochastic logic programming solver capable of executing these computations.

Biological neurons are a primary target for quantum information research, specifically for exploring how quantum mechanics might explain brain functions. This overview examines the current state of quantum data within the brain, including mechanisms for storing, processing, and transmitting this data. We also address the critical issue of decoherence and propose potential strategies to counteract these effects in the context of quantum neural systems.

In our work, we demonstrate that Ramanujan's equation applies to the Hurwitz zeta function, thereby offering multiple integral representations for polynomials in the Hurwitz zeta function.

This approach extends the spectral flow formulation of free fermionic systems, replacing simple equivariance with logical equivariance. We demonstrate that $H^{*,*}_{\text{log-eq}}(\text{SU}(2))$ offers a more comprehensive set of invariant data compared to prior invariants derived through logical equivariance. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between this new invariant and $K$-theory, alongside $K$-theoretic free fermionic models that generalize the Kitaev chain.

This work details the NLO QLO calculation of total cross-sections and angular distributions for $J/\psi$ production in association with $\eta_c$ and $\chi_{cJ}$ mesons ($J=0,1,2$) via $e^+e^-$ annihilation. Calculations were performed at center-of-mass energies near 10.6 GeV, specifically modeling conditions at the BEPCII collider. The NQLO q̄c amplitude analysis indicates that these contributions align with both previous experimental measurements and theoretical expectations.

This paper investigates how Signal enthusiasts and casual users comprehend the security of PINs. Through a combination of interviews and a lab experiment, we examined user understanding and found that while most participants view PINs as passwords, they often lack awareness that these codes serve as session authentication. Many users employ memorable yet easily guessable numbers, and some attempt to use them across multiple devices. Additionally, the data reveals that even among Signal enthusiasts, there is confusion regarding the nature of session PINs. We conclude by offering practical recommendations to enhance user behavior and clarity.

This study introduces a novel, streamlined methodology for solving the solar-power integration problem. We employ Gaussian quadrature, adapted to transform the standard integral into a wighted form with solar energy as the basis function. The proposed algorithm generates Gaussian quadrature coefficients and weights within the specified interval. Our method's accuracy is demonstrated through the solution of 30 test cases with varying degrees of difficulty. We have also incorporated the solution with the "P. Sand" power system, demonstrating its application.

Relying exclusively on point clouds for processing 3D surfaces is a common challenge, yet these shapes often possess complex curvature that is essential for downstream tasks. While curvature offers critical geometric insights, existing methods struggle with efficient curvature integration. This paper introduces a new algorithm designed to perform curvature estimation directly on the point cloud data. The core of this work is a novel optimization strategy based on the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) method applied within a low-rank framework. This method facilitates the simultaneous estimation of Gaussian curvature and Mean curvature across various surfaces. Theoretically, this approach is supported by a convergence proof, and experimental results on diverse datasets confirm the method's accuracy and efficiency.

In many major Indo-European languages, nouns are assigned a grammatical gender that influences the interpretation of nouns by language models. This study investigates how such gender assignment affects neural representations. We trained a multilingual model on a gender-marked corpus and observed that while noun embeddings captured clear and distinct gender characteristics, these were not uniform across the lexicon. Instead, we found that the strength with which a noun encoded gender information varied based on the frequency of gender-markers within that specific noun form. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these patterns hold true even when analyzing individual contexts.

We examine the deformations of the constant arithmetic group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathcal{O}_F)$, where $\mathcal{O}_F$ denotes the ring of integers of a number field $F$. These deformements are analyzed via their associated cohomology groups, which we term "chamability" groups. Our findings indicate that for $n=2$, deformations are invariably trivial, whereas for $n\geq 3$, they may be non-trivial. Specifically, we establish that stiffness fails for the constant special linear group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ whenever $n\geq 3$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the endomorphism ring of an elementary matrix group is a principal ideal domain.

Accurately estimating the position of objects from an image is crucial for various robotics tasks, such as manipulation and navigation. While existing methods are effective for known object categories, they struggle with unseen categories. This limitation stems from the reliance on training data, which necessitates extensive manual annotation for each new category to ensure robustness. To address this, we introduce a new approach for estimating object positions in zero-shot scenarios. Our method involves two key components: (1) training an object position estimator using a diverse range of categories to enhance generalization, and (2) employing a multi-modal approach to mitigate biases inherent in specific data modalities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in zero-shot object position estimation. The source code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/PrincetonVRLab/zero-shot-obj-pos-estim}.

Accurately forecasting traffic patterns is essential for urban infrastructure management, public policy formulation, and traffic control systems. However, conventional statistical and machine learning techniques typically require dense data inputs, which are difficult to obtain in urban traffic environments where information is naturally sparse. This paper introduces a novel approach to traffic forecasting that leverages similarity, allowing models to function effectively with sparse data by utilizing historical patterns from other similar locations rather than relying solely on local information. We evaluate the proposed method against established baselines using real-world datasets and demonstrate its superior performance. Additionally, to address the computational challenges of executing models across large city-wide networks, we develop an optimized algorithm that significantly accelerates training speeds without compromising forecast accuracy.

This paper introduces VACA, a class of variational graph autoencoders designed for learning causal representations capable of addressing both interventional and counterfactual queries. Causal representation learning extends beyond simple interprediction by incorporating capacity for inference regarding interventional and contrafactual scenarios. While recent graph neural networks have effectively handled the descriptive aspect of causal modeling, the corresponding inferential functionalities remain largely unexplored. Furthermore, the existing graph autoencoders that support causal inference rely on variational techniques derived from probabilistic methods, often resulting in high computational costs. In contrast, our proposed VACA utilizes variational encoding within a causal framework to achieve significant efficiency gains. We demonstrate that VACA surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both accuracy and speed, while remaining sufficiently flexible to be adapted for various specialized applications.

This paper details the initial results from the Irish LOFAR station's new REAL-time Transient Acquisition backend, REALTA. REALTA is designed to identify fast radio bursts (FRBs) and other rapidly changing transient signals, operating at speeds of up to 100 million samples per second to analyze single pulses lasting as briefly as 100 nanoseconds. The system's capabilities were validated using data from simulated transients and archived observations from LOFAR. Metaphotonics utilize surface plasmons to leverage their subwavelength confinement and intense light-matter coupling for diverse photonic applications. As this emerging field matures, researchers are increasingly adopting computational techniques to design and discover novel plasmonic architectures. Although machine learning (ML) has been applied to various electromagnetic problems, its efficacy in metaphotonics remains limited, hindered by the scarcity of high-quality training data. This paper introduces a strategy to overcome this limitation by generating training datasets through electromagnetic simulations, which are then leveraged to train a neural network for modeling complex plasmonic responses. Leveraging this approach, we demonstrate the capability to perform complex, non-trivial tasks within metaphotonics, including the engineering of intricate metamaterials, the optimization of complex plasmonic systems, and the analysis of circulating surface plasmons. These results highlight the transformative role of data-driven methodologies in advancing metaphotonics, suggesting a future where ML and metaphotonics converge to usher in a new era of metaphotonics.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,000 films from the past decade to enable robust analysis. We explore how various pre-release attributes influence box office revenue, findings which indicate that while these metrics are weak predictors of revenue on their own, they become more meaningful when considered together. Additionally, we examine the disparity between genre-specific and temporal trends, revealing that certain attributes function differently across genres or have shifted in importance over specific time periods. Our results underscore the necessity of integrating multiple factors when forecasting revenue, particularly given the varying significance of attributes across different genres and eras.

This research investigates the low-frequency swing phenomena inherent to electrical power grids. We develop a dynamic framework where the grid's electrical characteristics are treated as time-varying, driven by a nonlinear oscillator operating under time-delayed frequency regulation. Through a linearized analysis of this model, and by applying techniques from delay differential equations, we derive explicit stability conditions for a new class of control strategies. Finally, to validate our theoretical findings, we present numerical simulations that demonstrate the model's applicability to actual power grid scenarios.

The advent of intelligent cyberphysical networks (ICPNs) is set to transform the operational paradigms of both cyber and cyberphysical infrastructures. ICPNs are defined by their capacity to integrate intelligent agents directly into both the physical components and the communication networks that link them. A primary objective within ICPNs is to embed intelligence throughout all system elements, enabling distributed decision-making among these agents. This approach fosters enhanced resilience and adaptability, ensuring that individual system responses can be dynamically modified in reaction to external disturbances. This work provides an overview of ICPNs, highlighting their distinguishing characteristics and potential applications. Furthermore, it examines critical research challenges and emerging directions within this field, with a specific focus on communication network design tailored for cyberphysical environments populated by intelligent agents.

This paper examines a novel Monte Carlo algorithm, introduced in a prior study, designed to simulate external-Compton scattering events involving both UV and soft X-ray photons, alongside their associated polarization angles. We evaluate this method's performance by applying it to UV and X-ray data from the blazar PKS 1222+316, which was observed by the Swift satellite. The study utilizes observations spanning three distinct epochs: 2005, 2006, and 2007. The simulation results indicate that the new algorithm accurately reproduces the observed spectral energy distributions and polarization vectors for each epoch. Furthermore, the derived physical parameters—including the number density of UV and soft X-ray photon fields, the anisotropy of these fields, and the orientation of the corresponding polarization angles—align with the values predicted by standard theoretical models.

We introduce a new algorithm for computing the Hessian of arbitrary-order derivatives across complex landscapes, relying on finite-difference methods and complex function theory. By leveraging Cauchy's differentiation formula, the algorithm obtains analytic extensions of functions and their higher derivatives along the unit circle in the complex plane; subsequently, matrix diagonalization yields the Hessian eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Performance evaluations demonstrate that this approach accurately handles random functions with noise, and it is effective even for probability density distributions lacking smoothness in the complex plane, as well as for potential functions resulting from molecular dynamics simulations.

We investigate the optimal sequential discrimination of two pure quantum states subject to random permutations, where one sequence of measurements is fixed and the other involves a random ordering. We demonstrate that an adaptive measurement strategy outperforms all non-adaptive approaches. We also establish that the two states are orthogonal if and only if their Bhattacharyya distance equals one. We further show that the sum of their eigenvalues raised to the power of $p$ remains constant for all $p \in [0, \infty)$, regardless of the specific unitary operators defining the states. Additionally, we confirm that their ranks are always two.

The quantized breakup of a helical QCD string, or "T-string," arising from heavy-ion collisions, serves as a mechanism for generating baryons. We have developed a quantized model for the fragmentation of this helical string to calculate the distinct production cross-sections of antibaryons and mesons for every flavor. The model incorporates the constraints of quantized angular momentum and surface charge density along the string to determine specific breaking points and the quantum states of resulting particles. Baryons are conceptualized as open strings with ends carrying fundamental color charges, while the string's rotation induces a surface charge that interacts via the non-abelian Corbino effect, causing it to break at points of charge accumulation. Additionally, the string ends are fixed at the endpoints of the color flux tube connecting the initial di-baryon system. The resulting particle yields depend on the quantized angular momentum and the specific breaking points, with all parameters calibrated to match experimental data. The model successfully replicates the relative yields of antibaryons to mesons and the specific flavor distributions for both particles.

Recent helioseismic studies have observed systematic north-south asymmetries in travel-time measurements, which some researchers attribute to the Sun's large-scale magnetic fields. This work investigates the potential of these magnetic currents to generate such asymmetries by analyzing data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) aboard NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). We identified 100 current systems near active regions over a 13-year period and calculated their impact on travel-time measurements using a forward model. The results indicate that these magnetic currents produce a mean systematic difference in north-south travel times of 0.02 ms, with a standard deviation of 0.04 ms. This estimated effect is consistent with the magnitudes found in recent helioseismic research.

Light field technology has gained significant traction in recent years due to its capacity to capture both spatial and angular viewpoints, thereby delivering a more immersive visual experience. However, this capability introduces complex data dimensions that challenge existing image compression techniques. To address this, we introduce a practical model for 3D light field image compression that leverages deep learning. Central to our approach is a parallax-aware framework designed to capture the non-linear relationship between pixel displacement and the variance in parallax across different light field images. By integrating this model into a deep learning system, our method achieves a balance between compression ratios and reconstruction fidelity. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique surpasses traditional methods in both rate-distortion performance and compression efficiency when applied to real-world light field images.

The primary objective is to harness the robust semantic encoding of the larger non-interactive model and the dynamic query-context interaction capabilities of the interactive component. The cross-lingual retrieval system is evaluated using a subset of the WS2020 dataset, where the Babels7 dataset is utilized to train the interaction sub-model. This work investigates the utility of employing quantum systems to execute a binary choice wagering task inspired by the game of chicken. We demonstrate that adopting an open system perspective allows a player to secure winnings exceeding the unit threshold, provided a specific condition is satisfied. Furthermore, we establish a continuous variable implementation for this game, wherein the player can achieve a winning probability approaching unity.

This study investigates the electronic and optical characteristics of stacked monolayers within the MA$_2$Z$_4$ family (M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; Z = N, P, As), utilizing first-principles calculations. The results indicate that the quasiparticle band alignment in these materials is stacking-independent, featuring a type-II staggered heterojunction structure. This architecture enables efficient charge separation and the formation of stacking-independent excitons. Furthermore, first-principles many-body perturbation theory reveals strong optical anisotropy, which is contingent upon the specific stacking arrangement.

An analysis of the 18 fb$^{-1}$ data collected by the LHCb experiment in 2010 and 2011 reveals a potential unusual process where a positive sigma decays into a proton and a pair of oppositely charged muons. The observed number of events is 11.7 $\pm$ 2.7 (stat) $\pm$ 1.7 (syst), which is consistent with 11.7 $\pm$ 2.7 (stat) $\pm$ 1.7 (syst) when accounting for systematic errors. This measurement is based on a lower limit on the branching fraction of $9.1 \times 10^{-8}$ at a 90% confidence level. The corresponding significance of this result is 3.8 standard deviations.

The formation of planetary systems relies on the development of gas protoplanetary disks around young stars. These disks typically emerge from prestellar cores during their transition to protostars, yet the specific mechanisms governing their creation remain poorly understood. This study utilizes high-resolution 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to track the full evolutionary path from prestellar core to protoplanetary disk, focusing on a core with magnetization levels comparable to those observed today. We find that disk formation is driven by magnetic braking, which facilitates angular momentum loss and core collapse. As the core contracts, magnetic pressure and magnetic reconnection events heat the gas, causing it to expand and temporarily stall the collapse. Eventually, gravity prevails, leading to the birth of a protostar and the rapid accretion of surrounding material. This process results in the swift formation of a small, hot, and massive disk. Over time, viscous cooling and magnetic field evolution allow the disk to contract and cool further, settling into a state resembling those seen in young stellar objects.

Atmospheric dispersion (AD) is a critical factor in high-precision spectroscopy, particularly within the context of radial velocity measurements. This study introduces a novel methodology for characterizing AD by modeling the atmosphere as a collection of discrete layers. Each layer is defined by its thickness, temperature, and refractive index, with the optical properties of each stratum calculated using the Edlen equation. The total AD is derived by integrating the atmospheric path through all layers. The primary objective is to determine the idealized parameters for atmospheric simulation that replicate observed AD when applied to radial velocity simulations. This work represents the initial phase of a three-part series; the second part will detail the simulation technique, and the third will evaluate the results.

This study addresses the challenge of predicting a sequence of related time series within a multi-period framework. We introduce a new Bayesian Time Series Varying Coefficient (BTVVC) model, which accounts for temporal lags and utilizes B-spline functions to capture evolving coefficients over time. By employing a Bayesian approach with BIC-based Bayesian spike-and-slab priors, the method facilitates model selection and variable screening. Variational inference is utilized to efficiently approximate complex, high-dimensional posterior distributions. The performance of the proposed model is validated through simulations and an analysis of real-world data.

Constant logic serves as a powerful framework for understanding the model theory of structured Pontryagin duals. This paper demonstrates that within this logical system, the connection between a group and its Stone–Čech compactification via power operations is both surprising and profound.

Federated learning (FL) is a machine learning approach that trains models across distributed devices while keeping local data private. While FL is renowned for mitigating data bias and minimizing privacy risks through privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy (DP), the integration of DP often exacerbates model fairness. This study evaluates how DP influences fairness in FL by applying the adaptive L2-regularization method, a common approach to implement differential privacy. We conducted experiments using the Adult and German credit datasets to analyze the interplay between privacy levels, fairness, and utility. Our findings indicate that enhancing data privacy through DP frequently compromises fairness, particularly in scenarios where training data is imbalanced.

We examine the phenomenology of the supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ model, which incorporates a right-handed Majorana neutrino. This framework, featuring gauge singlet neutrinos, is highly attractive due to its simplicity and its ability to remain consistent with current experimental data. Specifically, it allows for a light sterile neutrino mass at the MeV scale, offering a viable solution to the dark matter and dark energy problems. We analyze the renormalization group evolution of $Z_2$ parity and the stability of the electroweak scalar potential, while also discussing the model's implications for supersymmetric dark matter detection at the Large Hadron Collider.

This study investigates a wireless network integrating interference management and intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) assisted device-to-device energy transfer. Specifically, it examines a setup where energy is transmitted from a source node to an energy harvesting device via an IRS, subsequently forwarding harvested energy to a data transmission device while coexisting with an independent data link. Addressing the complexity of the non-convex optimization problem for simultaneous energy harvesting and power allocation, the paper introduces a deep unsupervised learning approach. This method is designed to learn the optimal patterns of energy harvesting and power distribution directly from a set of interference channel coefficients. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed deep unsupervised framework achieves performance on par with existing benchmark schemes.

This study examines the first-forbidden beta decay of $^{186}$Hg, a process notable for being the inaugural observation of a first-forbidden transition from a spin-0 parent state to a spin-1 daughter. The investigation analyzes the decay's spectral shape across the entire energy range and, for the first time, provides a detailed analysis of the low-energy region. The findings, when compared to theoretical models, yield a first experimental determination of the $g_1/A$ factor for this specific class of forbidden decay. Additionally, the study reports measurements of the isomeric ratio, the nuclear recoil energy, and the beta-n-gamma angular correlation. The measured nuclear recoil aligns with theoretical predictions, while the beta-n-gamma correlation offers a novel method for extracting the delta $J$ $= 1$ shape factor. The isomeric ratio is found to be in good agreement with predictions from theoretical calculations.

We introduce a unified framework where the dark matter (DM) relic density and the baryon asymmetry (BA) of the cosmos originate from the decay of a single baryon-symmetric fermionic mediator. This mediator couples to both a fermionic dark matter candidate and the Standard Model leptons. In this model, the observed DM abundance is determined by the DM relic density, which depends on the mass of this mediator and its coupling to dark matter fermions. Specifically, if the interaction between the mediator and dark matter is sufficiently strong, the DM particle experiences annihilation to levels that exceed those predicted by freeze-out, thereby reducing the final relic density to match observational constraints. Furthermore, the mediator's leptonic decay channels drive leptogenesis. We demonstrate that the magnitude of the baryon asymmetry can be adequately explained by the CP-violating processes occurring during these decays.

We introduce a novel framework for learning control policies by integrating physical models with deep reinforcement learning (DRL). This hybrid approach utilizes a data-driven dynamic model to estimate control outcomes, enabling the use of very small datasets and side information to achieve rapid learning. Specifically, we trained a motion model using a limited data collection process that incorporated sensor measurements and actuator commands to predict states. This predictive model serves a dual purpose: it accelerates the learning of a policy through deep reinforcement learning and allows for model-based control optimization. We validated this approach on a flapping-wing robot, demonstrating that our method successfully acquires complex behaviors like reaching, swimming, flying, and walking with significantly fewer data samples than traditional methods. Furthermore, the generated policies are robust against environmental changes and hardware faults. The model's generalization capabilities are demonstrated across diverse robots, including a walking quadruped and flapping flying platforms featuring different morphologies and actuation systems.

We examine the three-dimensional $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, establishing analogs to Ward identities found in two-dimensional Toda models. These analogs involve integrals over three-dimensional space over which the total energy-momentum tensor vanishes pointwise, thereby transforming the Ward relations into constraints on spatial integration domains. We explicitly calculate and present the formulas for charges associated with the generators of the underlying symmetry algebra.

Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) excel at generating realistic single images, they struggle with the challenge of realistic relationship synthesis. To overcome this, the Relation GAN (RGAN) was introduced to effectively learn relationships within image pairs. However, training RGAs remains difficult because generating realistic relationships is more complex than creating realistic images, often leading to the "good relationship collapse" issue where discriminators fail to distinguish between real and fake relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce the Triplet-RGAN (TRGAN), a novel framework that leverages triplet loss to enhance adversarial training. By aligning this approach with the principles of metric learning, our method resolves the discrimination failure problem. Furthermore, we incorporate an auxiliary task to bolster the expressiveness of the generator. Experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that TRGAN surpasses existing methods, achieving superior performance in both image quality and the realism of generated relationships.

Quantum key exchange (QKE) facilitates the generation of secret keys between two parties, leveraging the fundamental laws of physics to prevent eavesdroppers from intercepting the keys without detection. A recent development in this field is the Twin-field QKE scheme, which achieves linear scaling of secret key rates relative to transmission distance and outperforms the standard BB84 protocol in highly lossy environments. However, the BB84-like variant of Twin-field QKE necessitates a phase-locking system between senders, creating technical complexities and potential security vulnerabilities. This study demonstrates that the BB84-free version of Twin-field QKE can operate effectively in both laboratory and field settings by eliminating the requirement for sender phase alignment. Experimental results confirm that the phase-absence configuration yields secret key rates consistent with the phase-locking arrangement, thereby validating its practicality.

Identifying objects within a scene is a fundamental yet difficult task in computer vision, primarily because training a robust system typically requires extensive labeled datasets. To address this limitation, this study introduces a novel approach called "pseudo bounding-box learning" designed to facilitate object identification. By leveraging image segmentation data, we automatically generate approximate bounding-box annotations to augment training data. Utilizing these generated "pseudo" labels, we train an integrated system that performs both semantic segmentation and object identification simultaneously. This method demonstrates significant success in open-vocabulary scenarios, achieving substantial performance gains without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Furthermore, we have released the source code to facilitate future research.

Transformer-based models have become essential in current research and applications, primarily due to their efficacy in generating high-quality outputs. However, a significant limitation is their susceptibility to producing inaccurate statements, which severely impacts real-world deployment. This paper offers a comprehensive review of existing literature addressing veracity in Transformers. We categorize prior research into three main areas: (1) assessing the likelihood of Transformer-generated text being incorrect, (2) generating veracious statements through optimized Transformer models, and (3) identifying and correcting inaccuracies in Transformer-produced text. Additionally, the study outlines promising future research avenues and provides a detailed analysis of current challenges within the field of Transformer text veracity.

This study addresses forecasting future deaths with an extensive dataset of monthly mortality counts, spanning 18 age and sex categories over the last 20 years, derived from 119 nations. We propose a time-varying factor model, where temporal factors fluctuate continuously and are approximated via splines. The corresponding time-invariant factor model, where factors remain constant, is solved using an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. Both approaches are evaluated against the classical Poisson model, with the time-varying model demonstrating superior predictive accuracy. Notably, the time-invariant model fails to adequately capture the observed mortality dynamics, particularly regarding the second factor. We posit that this factor represents the impact of COVID-19, which exhibits a delayed, lumpy, and non-linear response across nations and age groups.

This work investigates the pervasive issue of search space interference in neural architecture search (NAS), which constrains the algorithm's ability to identify optimal architectures. We first demonstrate that interference is inherent to current search space designs, significantly degrading performance by diminishing the diversity of the resulting models. Furthermore, we propose a novel, data-driven methodology to quantify interference levels. Experimentally, we show that interference persists across various search space structures and NAS algorithms. To mitigate these effects, we introduce an automated framework for designing custom, custom-tailored NAS search spaces. This framework minimizes interference through an iterative process that leverages model evaluations to refine the architecture. Evaluations on the NAS-Bench-201 benchmark confirm that our approach substantially outperforms prior methods, yielding more diverse and higher-quality neural architectures.

Extracting and analyzing time series features is a fundamental step in many time series modeling workflows. This article introduces the R package `timeSeriesFeatures` (referred to in this work as theft), which offers functionality for generating, managing, and visualizing time series feature sets.

We present a cohomological criterion that determines when a cohomologically locally compact CAT(0) space shares cohomology with its boundary. This result extends earlier work by Borel and Serre, as well as Eckmann and Weinberger. Following this, we offer a simple, cohomologically locally CAT(0) condition under which a geodesically complete space has a cohomology ring isomorphic to that of a product of its boundary and the non-negative real line. This characterization generalizes a result by Bridson and provides non-trivial examples of such spaces, notably certain solvable Lie groups.

We introduce a straightforward and adaptable statistical approach for evaluating translators' reliability using Bayesian methodology. This technique incorporates relevant prior knowledge about a translator's capabilities and produces a concise metric indicating their overall reliability. We examine how this added informational foundation influences the precision of that reliability assessment and demonstrate the method's application through a practical example.

Using principles from spectral theory, we establish two sum rules that describe the integrals of the leading eigenfunctions associated with scattering absorptions. These fundamental rules are demonstrated to be especially effective for determining the total, energy-dependent deposition of energy within an inhomogeneous medium when subject to an external source. The approach is validated through its application to modeling energy deposition in targets composed of distinct spheres of varying materials embedded within a solvent. Energy deposition profiles are visualized through one-dimensional charts displaying the ten most significant eigenchannels against a gradient of varying sphere concentrations.

Pruning has emerged as a highly effective strategy for compressing deep neural networks, yielding performance improvements that rival or exceed those of more intricate deep learning architectures. This paper examines the hypothesis that the most effective pruning technique involves identifying and retaining only the essential weights. We demonstrate that, within the context of the Pruning Lottery Ticket, this selection process aligns with the core principles of convolutional networks. Consequently, this provides a compelling rationale for the widespread adoption of convolutions in deep learning, highlighting that such architectures can effectively sift out non-informative weights to enhance efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce a streamlined pruning approach that integrates sparsity with a shallow optimization layer, achieving results on par with standard convolutions. This method offers a highly efficient and rapid alternative for deploying deep neural networks.

This paper introduces a new framework for analyzing lottery games that accounts for the anticipated actions of rational participants. We define "anti-clone" strategies as approaches that maximize the prize value of individual winnings. We demonstrate that anti-clone strategies are guaranteed to exist for every lottery format. For many common types of lotteries, we provide specific algorithms capable of generating these anti-clones. Furthermore, we establish a set of rules determining the optimal timing for buying lottery tickets. Finally, we illustrate our methods with a detailed analysis of 6/49-style lotteries.

We present the computation of the six-loop anomalous dimension for the $\phi^Q$ operator within the $O(N)$ symmetric model, where $d = 6 - \epsilon$. This result enables the calculation of the $\epsilon$-dependent part of the $\phi^Q$ operator's anomalous dimension $\gamma_{\phi^Q}$. Additionally, the universal fixed-point value of the $\phi^Q$ scaling exponent $\lambda_{\phi^Q} = d + \gamma_{\phi^Q}$ is derived for the specific case of critical multicomponent Heisenberg spins ($Q=1$, $N=3$). Finally, the $\lambda_{\phi^Q}(\text{Heisenberg})$ result is compared with the previously computed $\lambda_{\phi^P}(\text{Heisenberg})$ and $\lambda_{\phi^P}(\text{Ising})$ values.

Valley degrees of freedom are crucial for the emerging field of valleytronics, a discipline analogous to spintronics but centered on utilizing valley-based properties for information processing. While electron-phonon interactions are recognized as a primary mechanism for controlling valley states, they also cause rapid valley relaxation. A significant challenge in experimental settings is distinguishing between intrinsic valley decay and processes influenced by environmental factors. In this study, we investigate how distinct electron-phonon coupling mechanisms affect valley dynamics in two-dimensional materials. We demonstrate that the isotropic deformation potential drives fast valley relaxation, whereas the novel valley-Kramers polarization (valley-KP) mechanism can substantially extend relaxation times. Furthermore, we illustrate how dielectric anisotropy influences these dynamics and propose a testable protocol to identify the valley-KP effect through experimental measurements.

We present an approach to unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection that leverages the joint modeling of appearance and geometry through a unified framework. By applying a cycle-consistent learning strategy, we develop CycleGeometryAdapt (CGA), which achieves superior results on the Unsupervised Object Detection benchmark of the NeurIPS 2022 challenge. Specifically, our method achieves a 56.2% mAP, marking a 6.8% absolute improvement over the best semi-supervised baseline and establishing a new state-of-the-art for this task.

Dimensionality reduction is a technique that projects high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space to reveal its inherent structure. t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a widely adopted method for visualizing such data. However, the original formulation is restricted to Euclidean spaces, preventing its direct application to other common manifolds, such as the hypersphere. This paper introduces Spherical t-SNE (VMF-SNE), an extension of the classic algorithm designed for spherical data representations. The proposed method leverages the Spherical Type-1 Matrix Variate distribution to model the upper hemisphere and the Spherical Type-2 Matrix Variate distribution to model the lower hemisphere. We empirically validate the effectiveness of this approach on synthetic data and the Google Image Spherical dataset, demonstrating that the resulting embeddings are superior to t-SNE and other existing spherical methods.

We have employed the diagrammatic Monte Carlo technique to investigate the fermicolaron within a two-dimensional weakly interacting Fermi gas, utilizing a large-scale, high-precision computation. Our results demonstrate that, across all interaction strengths, the polaron exists in a stable state free of bound states. Specifically, as the attractive force intensifies, the excitations associated with the energy denominator in the perturbation expansion increasingly dominate the calculation of the energy shift. Consequently, conventional diagrammatic approaches are likely to become computationally prohibitive for strongly interacting regimes. To resolve this issue, we suggest modifying the perturbative framework to incorporate dominant diagrams through a reorganization of the expansion, thereby enabling Monte Carlo sampling of the remaining, standard diagrams.

This paper introduces a hybrid digital–analog quantum computing architecture specifically tailored to simulate fermionic systems. At its core, the approach integrates the digital fermionic density matrix embedding theory (FDMET) algorithm with analog gate operations. Leveraging the quantum analog control theory, we demonstrate that a single-qubit digital fermionic operation—implemented via fermionic gates—can be efficiently emulated through continuous quantum dynamics. This methodology is applicable to both discrete (Type I) and continuous (Type II) fermionic systems. To validate our framework, we computed the ground-state energy for the one-dimensional Hubbard model and the BCS pairing energy gap across various system sizes. Our results show that the hybrid analog emulation yields exact Fermionic digital outcomes, confirming the accuracy of the approach.

Graph polynomials serve as essential tools for characterizing graphs through specific numerical values. This paper examines various graph properties that correspond to the locations of roots for these polynomials. We establish upper limits on the count of graphs where the graph independence polynomial has roots in the unit disk, as well as the number of graphs with a self-complementary status sharing this trait. Additionally, our findings address the graph matching polynomial and the algebraic connectivity of graphs relative to Fiedler's Laplacian matrix.

The Veech curve $\mathcal C_V$ within the moduli space $\mathcal H(2,2,2)$ of hyperelliptic curves with signature $(2,2,2)$ is defined as the locus of Jacobians corresponding to stable curves formed by the union of three elliptic curves intersecting in two points. This study investigates the central divisors arising from these curves. Our findings demonstrate that the central divisors associated with the union of three elliptic curves at their generic Jacobian configurations are congruent modulo the central divisors of the resulting elliptic curves.

To achieve this, we employ the method of elliptic curves decomposition, which involves decomposing the Jacobian variety $\mathcal{J}(E_1 + E_2 + E_3)$ into the tensor product of the individual elliptic curve components $E_1, E_2$, and $E_3$. This factorization holds whenever the sum of three elliptic curves is considered in a generic position.

In addition, we examine the specific case where $E_1 + E_2 + E_3$ lies on the Veech curve $\mathcal C_V$ and two of these curves possess an isomorphic structure. This scenario is analyzed using the decomposition of the Prym variety associated with the bi-elliptic double cover of $E_1 + E_2 + E_3$ at its branch points.
