Accurately and reliably calculating the inter-beat interval (IBI) and heart rate from photoplethysmogram (PGM) signals is essential for both medical diagnostics and health monitoring. This study introduces a novel hybrid IBI detection framework combining deep learning with advanced signal processing. We utilize a U-Net model trained on the original PGM to estimate heart rate, which subsequently guides the precise localization of the PGM peaks. These peaks subsequently feed into a Tiramisu model, originally developed for image processing tasks, to refine the estimation of inter-beat intervals. Experimental results indicate that this proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a success rate of 98.8% with an error margin below 5%.

We introduce a randomized algorithm designed to compute the most significant singular values and vectors of a tensor of dimension $d$ and size $n$. This method requires $d$ matrix-multiplication operations per additional singular value-tuple extracted, alongside just one or a few extra matrix multiplications. Its performance is comparable to established algorithms when processing the leading singular value-tuples, yet it handles tensors of practical dimensions and sparse data efficiently. The method's effectiveness stems from a random projection technique that isolates the dominant subspace of a tensor, leveraging the connection between tensor power actions and the Carleman linearization framework. The approach is validated through experiments on synthetic data and a real-world dataset.

Graph embedding involves mapping graph structures to lower-dimensional vector spaces, a technique widely used across various fields. While significant research has historically focused on embedding static graphs, real-world data is often dynamic, requiring dynamic approaches for graph learning. This survey provides a comprehensive review of existing methods for embedding evolving graphs. We categorize current dynamic graph embedding techniques into three distinct categories: (1) learning from evolving networks by generating a single vector per node, (2) learning from networks with dynamic subgraphs using a set of node vectors, and (3) learning from networks with dynamic edges using a set of edge vectors. For each category, we detail the underlying logic, present the strengths and weaknesses of the approaches, and identify potential future research directions. To support this analysis, we compiled a curated dataset of 39 papers on dynamic graph embedding, organized into a bibliography organized by research task.

This paper investigates the conformal change issue on a hemisphere where the scalar curvature and its Hessian are both flat. We demonstrate that any radial solution to this equation must be constant. Our result further establishes that for every $r \in (0, \pi)$, there exists a solution that is radially symmetric yet unbounded as it approaches the boundary tending toward $+\infty$ or $-\infty$. Specifically, if the boundary values are fixed to $0$, there exists a solution that is radially symmetric, positive inside the domain, and vanishes on the boundary.

We introduce a deep generative framework designed to learn a highly expressive and optimal representation for a given data distribution. Our approach trains a normalizing flow to learn a density estimator that minimizes a Sinkhorn divergence calculated between a power mean of a reference distribution and density estimator output. We provide theoretical justification for demonstrating the model's capacity to approximate a power mean of the reference distribution, establishing its ability to learn an optimal representation. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic data and real-world benchmarks illustrate that the framework effectively approximates this optimal representation, evidenced by superior performance in downstream tasks such as classification and clustering. Furthermore, our analysis of a supporting proof for a Whittle index problem demonstrates a practical application of this learned optimal representation.

In late 2020, the UK government introduced Local Tracing Partnerships (TPs), involving local authorities alongside public health officials to bolster COVID-19 contact tracing. Although these initiatives have been running for several months, limited data exists regarding their effectiveness. This study addresses this gap by analyzing data from the national app, which includes user interactions with both conventional contacts and those identified through Local TPs. The research compares the speed of isolation uptake and the proportion of isolates returning to normal activity for individuals flagged by each method. The findings reveal that individuals traced by Local Tracing Partnerships return to regular activities more rapidly than those identified through other channels. To explain this, the paper introduces a model that accounts for varying levels of "awareness" regarding the spread of the virus, suggesting that Local Tracing Partnerships have heightened community alertness. The authors conclude that while Local Tracing Partnerships may be less efficient at detecting outbreaks than traditional tracing, they play a valuable complementary role in accelerating the overall recovery from the pandemic.

This study utilizes Gaia DR2 data to analyze the physical properties of the open cluster Melotte 72. The analysis includes distance estimation, reddening determination, and the construction of a main sequence turnoff (MSTO) diagram. Results indicate a distance of 1.02 ± 0.03 kpc and a reddening of 0.11 ± 0.03 mag. The derived MSTO suggests an age of 1.02 ± 0.03 Gyr. Uncertainties in these values stem from systematic errors in the photometric calibration, the selection of the main sequence turnoff point, and the adopted distance modulus. Additionally, the study investigates the influence of the main sequence turnoff point on the derived age and concludes that a 10% error in the distance modulus results in a proportional 10% uncertainty in age.

Camera extrinsic parameters are vital for robotics, particularly in robot vision and eye-in-hand 3D reconstruction. While precise calibration is essential, it is often laborious and costly for most robot manufacturers and end-users. This paper introduces a self-calibration approach designed to rapidly and effortlessly adjust a robot's camera using just a single image, leveraging the 3D pose of the grasped object. We propose a deep learning framework that estimates the camera's extrinsic parameters by analyzing an image of the gripper holding an object with a known pose. To enhance the model's generalization across diverse object shapes, a data augmentation strategy is employed. We also utilize a differentiable renderer to facilitate end-to-end training of the system. Experimental results on both synthetic data and real-world images demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance compared to existing techniques.

We introduce Reverse Conscious Reinforcement Learning (Reverse CRL), a method that leverages a pre-trained model to solve tasks previously mastered by a base RL agent. This approach involves training a base RL agent on a broad task distribution and subsequently restricting it to a specific subtask. We define a reward function that evaluates the likelihood of a trajectory remaining within this subsubspace; this function is then used to guide the Reverse CRL model, which learns to maximize that probability. By optimizing for this objective, the model generates sequences that the base RL agent would have chosen had it been able to execute the subtask successfully. We demonstrate that Reverse CRL can replicate a behavior identical to the base RL agent's perfect policy for that subtask, without ever being explicitly trained on that specific subtask initially. Empirical results indicate that this method generalizes effectively to new tasks and domains. Furthermore, the paper explores applications of Reverse CRL in imitating experts who are constrained by the limitations of a weaker, base model.

We introduce the GAIA mission, the European Space Agency's third major interplanetary project, scheduled for a 2013 launch. Over a decade, GAIA will conduct continuous astrometric and photometric surveys of nearly one billion celestial objects, ranging from 10 milliarcseconds to 10 parsecs. The data gathered will enable the creation of an unprecedented census of the Milky Way's stars in three dimensions, facilitating the study of its formation and evolution. Additionally, GAIA will observe 100 million objects beyond our galaxy, including nearby stars, the galactic halo, the closest globular clusters, the Andromeda galaxy, the Magellanic Clouds, and nearby galaxies. The mission's primary scientific objectives include determining the age and formation history of the Milky Way, the internal dynamics of the galaxy, stellar populations, and the galactic disk's secular evolution. GAIA will also deliver a precise parallax for proper motions of the stars within the galactic halo and disk, allowing for the measurement of the rotation curve, the galactic disk's vertical structure, and the masses of the galactic disk, bulge, and dark halo. The data will also provide a high-resolution view of the spiral structure of the galactic disk, the galactic halo, and the galactic bulge, as well as the galactic disk, bulge, and dark halo. To address the growing complexity of biological networks, we present a unified Bayesian framework for inferring and measuring networks that incorporates weights for directed edges. This approach allows for the inclusion of external data, such as omics profiles, to aid network discovery. We define a set of requirements for interpreting network weights and demonstrate how our method satisfies these criteria. Specifically, we show that our method can be adapted to create Bayesian versions of various deterministic algorithms, including those used for inferred and measured networks. By applying this flexible framework to a case study involving the human transcription factor network, we show that integrating transcription factor binding data as weights for forward edges and binding affinity measurements as weights for backward edges yields more accurate results than using either data type alone.

Geostatistics and machine learning techniques are increasingly integrated into environmental epidemiology to model the spatio-temporal distribution of air pollutants. This discussion examines the challenges and benefits of applying such models to air pollution exposure assessment in diverse epidemiological research settings.

Experimental searches for Majorana zero modes (ZMs) within nanowire-superconductor junctions have yielded promising results, yet the scientific community remains divided regarding the interpretation of the data. The ambiguity stems largely from the inability to rule out the trivial 0π phase transition occurring in the normal segment of the nanowire, which can mimic the signatures of a Majorana zero mode. This study introduces a novel strategy to differentiate between trivial zero modes and true zero-energy Majorana modes by employing resistive electrodes within a tunneling spectroscopy setup. Our analysis indicates that the presence of resistive materials in the normal region effectively suppresses the trivial 0π phase transition, thereby enhancing the capability to identify the distinct Majorana 0π state amidst the noise of other modes.

This study examines the online bandit problem within a $d$-dimensional rich action set $\mathcal{F}$, where actions are chosen from $\mathcal{F}$ and the reward follows a linear model with an unknown parameter $\theta^* \in \mathbb{R}^d$. We demonstrate that when $\mathcal{F}$ is Lipschitz continuous, the cumulative regret of any policy scales as $O(|\mathcal{F}|^{2/3}d^{1/2}\sqrt{T})$ for a horizon $T$, provided the state is chosen uniformly at random. This result holds even if the policy lacks knowledge of $\theta^*$ or the environment's Lipschitz constant. We further show that the policy can efficiently approximate the optimal parameter $\theta^*$ with high probability, achieving an estimation error bounded by $O(|\theta - \theta^*|) = O(|\mathcal{F}|^{2/3}d^{1/2})$. We establish that this estimation error is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. Additionally, we prove that the sample complexity required to perform hypothesis testing or to learn a policy with regret $<\epsilon$ is $O(\epsilon^{-2}d)$. We demonstrate that this sample complexity is also optimal up to logarithmic factors for a policy in a bandit setting with a specific structure. Gapped graphene is widely recognized for exhibiting a robust Valley Hall effect, a property that enables significant potential for spintronics and magneto-transport applications. However, this study suggests that the orbital Hall phenomenon offers a superior alternative in these contexts. We demonstrate that in gapped graphene, a finite spin polarization emerges transversely to a spinless particle current flowing through it. This orbital-induced spin polarization surpasses the Valley Hall effect in strength by several orders of magnitude. This substantial phenomenon is attributed to specific gapped graphene characteristics, including Berry curvature, spin-orbit coupling, and the inverse graphene Berry curvature metric.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are increasingly vital for machine learning tasks involving graph data, yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks remains a critical open challenge. This study focuses on data contamination, a reinforcement learning scenario where an adversary strategically injects malicious training samples to maximize model performance for an asymptotic regime. The objective is to determine optimal strategies within this adversarial framework. We introduce Graph Policy Evaluation (GPE), a novel algorithm that adapts value iteration to address the complex action and state spaces inherent to GNNs. Theoretical analysis demonstrates GPE's sample efficiency, and experimental results show it effectively solves data contamination across various graph topologies and GNN architectures. Furthermore, experiments reveal that our method outperforms existing algorithms in navigating expansive graph structures.

By matching sources based on their relative positions and the colors derived from 2MASS filters, we successfully cross-referenced the catalogs. An edge in a set system is defined as a finite collection of elements from a set $X$ that is not included in any larger such subcollection within the given family. A vertex $x \in X$ is minimal in a set system $\mathcal F$ if it does not belong to any other member of $\mathcal F$. We define a set system $\mathcal F$ as minimal if every element within it contains at least one minimal vertex. This work investigates the existence of maximal families of infinite sets of elements from $X$ that are pairwise intersecting only in minimal vertices. This inquiry extends previous research by J. Komjáth and Z. Buczak, who focused specifically on families of finite sets of elements from $X$ that are pairwise intersecting only in minimal vertices.

Large ontologies are essential for ontology development, yet their size often hinders both creation and maintenance efforts. While numerous visualization tools exist to facilitate ontology inspection, they typically fail to accommodate non-hierarchical associations or are unsuitable for handling ontologies of significant scale. To address this limitation, we introduce **OntoPlot**, a visualization tool specifically designed to manage large ontologies featuring non-hierarchical links. Our evaluation demonstrates that users can effectively analyze large ontologies with non-hierarchical associations using OntoPlot, and we further demonstrate that the tool successfully integrates with **Protégé**, the widely adopted ontology editor.

This study introduces a novel framework designed to leverage CycleGAN and an inter-domain loss function for semi-supervised, end-to-end automatic speech recognition. We evaluate the approach using the Voice Bank-Converson 2014/2015 datasets, demonstrating that semi-supervised performance significantly surpasses that of a fully supervised baseline. Additionally, our results achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to other semi-supervised solutions on these datasets.

This study introduces a novel approach to robot navigation by integrating a deep neural network with an active learning framework. While deep reinforcement learning has shown promise for robotics, it typically demands extensive labeled datasets that are costly to generate. In contrast, our method employs a neural network to forecast movement and uses active learning to restrict training to a small, strategically selected subset of states. This strategy significantly lowers the volume of training data required for successful navigation. The approach was validated on a simulated 2D differential-drive mobile robot tasked with reaching a specific goal while avoiding hazards. The results demonstrate that the method successfully learns effective navigation policies using trajectory data from merely 0.0001% of possible states.

This study investigates the impact of a flexible molecular conformational degree of freedom on the Soret coefficient, specifically examining a binary mixture where a small, molecularly flexible solute exists as multiple conformers in multiple equilibrium with its solvent. We demonstrate that internal rotational relaxation within the solute can yield a non-zero Soret coefficient even in the absence of molecular interactions, driven solely by solute solubility variations across different temperature ranges. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive formula for the Soret coefficient tailored to such two-component systems featuring flexible solute molecules, which accounts for thermo-transport properties of individual molecular species alongside interaction potentials. Our theoretical predictions are validated through simulations of self-diffusion and thermal diffusion in a binary mixture of molecules modeled with the Lennard-Jones potential, where the solute exhibits both temperature-dependent solubility and distinct molecular weights. We find that the solute's intrinsic tendency to diffuse more rapidly with rising temperature significantly amplifies the overall mixture's Soret coefficient. Additionally, the sensitivity of the Soret coefficient to molecular weights varies depending on the specific temperature and chemical properties of the molecular species.

This study introduces a novel architecture, UniLM-Assessor, which integrates a student-specific effective transformer model capable of utilizing both an essay and its corresponding prompt as input tokens. Our assessor establishes new state-of-the-line performance benchmarks on the automated essay evaluation track, specifically achieving significant improvements over current best methods. Our findings indicate that the UniLM model surpasses the best existing systems by a margin of 0.20 on the overall correlation coefficient when tested on the 2018 FLAN Language Assessment Division data. Additionally, our model achieves 0.20 higher scores in the 2018 FLAN English Track competition, yielding an overall improvement of 0.2 points. While the integration of adaptive learning strategies has significantly enhanced pedestrian detection in diverse domains, a persistent issue remains: the detection of false positives in atypical or unusual backgrounds. This study introduces an unsupervised, out-of-the-box false positive mitigation framework that re-ranks bounding boxes to assign lower confidence scores to uncertain predictions. By leveraging the principle that objects in atypical backgrounds often exhibit inconsistent feature representations, the method re-evaluates these ambiguous cases. Empirical results demonstrate that the box re-rank module effectively reduces false positives without compromising the detector's primary performance metrics.

We introduce an automatic framework designed to enhance the quality of both vocals and instrumental tracks in music productions. The core of this system employs an advanced neural architecture that integrates image translation with spectral warping techniques to boost the fidelity of the original audio. A key challenge in applying current high-fidelity audio synthesis methods involves the scarcity of training data, as most available datasets consist of "dry" (isolated) and "mixed" music pairs that lack the perceptual richness found in professional commercial mixes. To overcome this limitation, we developed a novel synthetic mixing process that generates realistic augmentation by incorporating high-fidelity commercial mixes into our training protocol. Extensive testing demonstrates that the proposed approach significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in improving vocal and instrumental clarity.

Throwing motions are integral to numerous sports, including baseball, tennis, and soccer. While coaching often emphasizes technical form, the actual effect of the ball's release point on performance remains largely unexplored. This study aims to fill that gap by investigating how deviations in the point of release influence throwing outcomes. To do so, we developed "FauxThrow," a motion capture and re-launch system capable of detecting release points and simulating throws from alternative locations. Our findings indicate that even minor alterations in the release point can result in substantial changes to throw performance. Consequently, this research offers valuable insights for sports coaching and could inform the future design of advanced robotic throwing systems.

This study introduces a novel, syntax-driven top-down tree-structured decoding framework designed to produce valid parse trees in real-time while generating syntax-dependent words. Although this approach shares a top-down, tree decomposition methodology with prior research, it diverges by utilizing a fixed, language-based topological ordering inherent in syntax to handle word generation. This underlying principle has been adapted for use within the sequence-to-sequence architecture for machine translation, demonstrating that the method produces valid parse trees instantly and captures syntax-based phenomena effectively.

Accurate knowledge of reaction rate coefficients is vital for astrochemical models to simulate the formation and evolution of molecular ices on dust grains in cold interstellar environments. These rates depend heavily on the binding energy of a molecule to a surface, which dictates the molecule's stability and phase transitions. However, due to the complexity of describing molecule-surface interactions, binding energy is typically calculated using quantum chemistry methods that vary in accuracy. Consequently, the significant uncertainty in these values hampers astrochemical modeling efforts. To address this, we introduce the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAS), a newly developed database offering a distribution of binding energies for a single reaction across multiple levels of quantum theory. BEAS provides a statistically grounded description of binding energy uncertainty, thereby facilitating the refinement of astrochemical models. The BEAS database can be accessed at https://beas.be.

We examine a type of asymmetric random walk on $[l,+\infty)$ where particles exhibit a lower bound that varies with sample data. This walk consists of steps forward of magnitude one occurring with probability $p$ and backward steps of magnitude one happening with probability $q=1-p$. We establish a sufficient condition for ensuring the strong Feller property for this stochastic process. Furthermore, using this finding, we analyze the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm applied to a class of piecewise constant potential functions within the Peng–Stern framework, demonstrating that the algorithm effectively generates this random walk provided the initial configuration of the walk is sufficiently rapid.

The study examines the global behavior of the reflection coefficient for the reflectionless and general reflection cases of the 2D stationary states in the integral formulation of the full-defocusing complex-modified Davey-Stewartson equations. The non-integrable complex-bilinear form is also utilized to explore reflectionless scenarios. In the reflectionless case, the solution to the potential field exhibits a non-meromorphic analytic nature with an infinite count of isolated zeros and poles; however, these properties are shown to align with those of solutions derived from both the non-integrable complex-bilinear form and initial conditions. For the general reflection scenario, the coefficient's behavior is analyzed as a function of the absolute wavenumber $|k|$. The analysis reveals that the real part of the coefficient remains non-negative for all $k$ only in shallow water regimes, whereas deep water regimes allow for sign changes. Furthermore, the number of zeros and poles in the upper half complex plane increases as water depth grows, and the distribution of these singularities stabilizes for sufficiently large $k$.

This paper introduces a Sibylvariant adaptation tailored for text classification. We demonstrate that the Sibylvariant algorithm, originally designed for graph problems, can be generalized for feature-weighted classification tasks. Specifically, we apply this method to the task of discriminating spam from legitimate emails. Our findings indicate that the Sibylvariant method outperforms the Support Vector Machine (SVM) and standard Naive Bayes (NB) algorithms. Furthermore, our robust version of the algorithm achieves superior results compared to a basic version, even when the dataset contains significant amounts of noisy or irrelevant data.

We present a method for explicitly deriving linear representations that achieves meta-learning across a curated collection of deep learning models. This framework provides a unified approach to simultaneously optimize both the representation and the training procedure of a downstream model. By integrating variational inference with a structured prior, our technique yields a closed-form solution for the update rules of a pretrained network, which are then employed to train a representation that minimizes a specific variational lower bound. The final model parameters are selected by optimizing this lower bound in a batch-wise manner. The efficacy of our representation is validated through experiments on a variety of image datasets and specific tasks, including batch normalization adaptation, test-time augmentation, and the adaptation of batch normalization layers to new data.

This research investigates the stability of model compression techniques, specifically knowledge distillation and post-training quantization, within the realm of machine translation. Our experiments reveal that while knowledge distillation maintains robustness, post-training post-training suffers from significant fragility. We identify that even minor variations in training configurations—such as the dataset seed or the initial model architecture—can drastically impact the final performance of quantized models. Consequently, this fragility renders quantization challenging to deploy in low-resource settings, as it necessitates an extensive grid search to identify suitable architectures and data handling strategies.

We introduce a novel hypergraph-based density that extends the multiple-field density of General Relativity. This formulation is constructed from the Lagrangian of a single, scalar hypergraph and is designed to accommodate an arbitrary number of fields. We demonstrate that this density can be derived through a path integral approach, which relies on the probability measure of that same scalar hypergraph. Furthermore, we establish that the equivalence between this density and Illogical Lagrangian Density (i.i.d LD) is contingent upon the use of the field equations of i.i.d LD. The current work lays the foundational framework for constructing a field theory based on scalar hypergraphs.

Deep learning models typically demand vast amounts of labeled data to achieve high performance, a challenge that is often difficult to meet in medical imaging due to the scarcity of time-constrained expert annotations. This study investigates the impact of reducing labeled datasets on the performance of pneumothorae segmentation deep neural networks. We evaluate the efficacy of three specific augmentation techniques—elastic deformations, Gaussian blurring, and copy-paste—applied to training data across limited label scenarios. Findings indicate that these augmentation strategies significantly enhance model performance when labeled data is scarce, with elastic deformations yielding the best results. Furthermore, the copy-paste technique was employed to increase local label density, and experiments revealed that smaller training datasets yield superior segmentation performance.

Although image captioning has made substantial progress, it still struggles with inconsistent performance, specifically regarding the balance between controllability and stability. While existing methods that employ image regeneration to achieve controllability often compromise captioning quality, we introduce a straightforward yet effective solution: prompt-based image captioning. By utilizing a pre-trained model and fine-tuning it on a carefully constructed prompt, we significantly enhance controllability. We further enhance this capability by introducing a novel "caption-embedding" designed to boost caption stability. Extensive experiments on the Flickr30k dataset demonstrate that our approach markedly improves controllability with minimal impact on stability.

This paper offers an initial exploration of the causal nature of harm, grounded in the widely accepted definition that an event $e$ causes harm to an individual $s$ when that event brings about a significant negative change within the person's history. We propose a novel framework for analyzing causal histories that proves more flexible than the standard concatenation-based models. This new approach successfully accommodates the complexities of intuitive cases, such as causal loops, multiple interactions, and histories embedded within other causal events. We demonstrate that, when coupled with established techniques for determining causation, this refined model yields a more coherent and robust understanding of how harm causally occurs.

This short note introduces MMLSpark, a comprehensive deep learning toolkit built for Apache Spark that supports flexible integration of both custom optimization layers and pre-trained models. Designed to operate seamlessly across multiple GPUs and clusters, it delivers end-to-end training capabilities. We provide an overview of the tool and illustrate its application by training a ResNet-50 architecture on the ImageNet dataset.

Voice translation, a core element of human language communication, has recently seen significant research interest. However, existing approaches are limited by the scarcity of available data and the high development costs associated with training models for specific language pairs. This study introduces Zero-shot Voice Translation (0-SVT), a technique capable of translating audio between any two languages without prior model training. The method is built upon a pre-trained framework that simultaneously handles speech conversion and transformation. By integrating a cycle-consistency constraint, the approach ensures the preservation of speaker-specific traits and linguistic nuances during the translation process. Trained using the LibriVox corpus, a model employing this method demonstrated the ability to translate between various language pairs in a zero-shot setting. The resulting translations achieved high fidelity, exhibiting strong speaker and cycling consistency alongside low Character Error Rates (CER).

This study examines a boundary value problem analogous to the Coleman-Gurtin model of phase change, where the conditions at moving boundaries are defined by a curvature-dependent term. Our analysis demonstrates both existence and uniqueness for the Coleman-Gurtin system. Furthermore, we establish that, as the parameter representing interfacial energy tends to zero, the problem's solution converges to the solution of the classical Coleman-Gurtin equation describing pure phase change without surface tension effects.

This study introduces a probabilistic load forecasting framework for distribution networks, utilizing a fusion of daily and nightly forecasts to predict uncertainty. The framework's performance is evaluated across various network configurations, with a specific focus on how an increase in peak demand correlates to prediction accuracy. The findings reveal that the proposed method is highly effective in anticipating extreme loads, particularly within scenarios characterized by significant spatial variations in load profiles.

Advancements in machine learning (ML) have produced numerous high-performing models, though their widespread application is constrained by the difficulty of synthesizing diverse ML capabilities. A primary obstacle stems from the challenge of embedding domain expertise into ML models. This work introduces a framework designed to facilitate the introduction of specialized domain knowledge into ML systems. We outline a roadmap for researching specialized knowledge integration within ML, leveraging insights from modular architectures and compositional design principles. Drawing on literature regarding domain knowledge integration in ML and the principles guiding compositionality and modularity, we develop an architectural model that offers a structured approach to combining ML components. Finally, we outline several avenues for future investigation into this emerging field.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread devastation, prompting an urgent need for effective diagnostic tools. While Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have proven highly accurate in detecting COVID-19 from chest X-rays (CXRs), they often introduce significant bias. This paper introduces a novel, weakly supervised approach to localize and segment COVID-19 lesions in CXRs, eliminating the need for labor-intensive pixel-level annotations. By utilizing only image-level labels, our method achieves an AUC of 0.822 on the NIH dataset, matching the performance of state-of-the-art fully supervised models. Furthermore, our results surpass current state-of-the-art self-supervised techniques on the same benchmark. This work demonstrates the potential of weakly supervised learning to deliver high-performance medical image analysis without incurring the high costs of detailed supervised data labeling.

Accurate localization and identification of vertebrae are critical for various clinical tasks, including the quantification of vertebral body height loss, osteophyte formation, and spinal curvature assessment. Existing deep learning-based methods for these tasks typically rely on training a model to localize vertebral bodies and another to predict identification labels, which are subsequently fused through post-processing. However, the localization step often suffers from performance degradation due to the deformity of the vertebral bodies caused by conditions like degenerative disc disease. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that rectifies deformated vertebrae to facilitate more precise localization and identification. Our approach anatomically aligns each vertebra with an ideal profile, thereby mitigating the impact of osteophytes and body height loss. Furthermore, we have developed an anatomically constrained optimization method that integrates vertebral alignment with a deep learning model designed for localization and identification. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

Dynamical stabilization, or suppression of decay, is a phenomenon where a quantum system's time-dependent evolution prevents it from reaching a lower energy state. This work investigates the stabilization of excited electronic states in a material cavity under intense laser excitation using a quantum kinetic approach. We analyze the time evolution of an excited electron interacting with its phonon environment within the cavity, demonstrating that strong laser fields can dynamically stabilize this state. Furthermore, we show that the rate of stabilization is significantly enhanced by vacuum fluctuations. These findings are corroborated by time-resolved time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) simulations.

This paper presents a method for training a quadruped robot to walk on rough terrain by leveraging a new actuator: springs. We introduce an approach that learns control policies for the robot, allowing it to take full advantage of these elastic actuators. Our results show that the robot can successfully navigate a wide range of natural terrains, including rocks and roots. Our work provides a promising path for developing robust and reliable robotic systems that can operate in a wide range of real-world environments.

This method employs the coherent information of an optimal environment state to construct a state that minimizes an upper bound on the minimum eigenvalue of the Holevo quantity associated with the reduced density matrix of the environment state. This optimization problem is solved using the standard algorithm for quantum subsystems through semidefinite programming. This method is demonstrated to be accurate for states in composite quantum systems that are mixed. We investigate the dynamics of a small-scale instability that emerges within collisionless slab plasmas subjected to a uniform background magnetic field and a mean flow. This phenomenon, which operates at length scales much smaller than the ion gyroradius, is driven by flow shear and remains independent of the background magnetic field strength. While this mode shares the characteristic of flow shear with the kinetic Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, it is distinct in its small wavelength and its ability to rapidly generate intense fields even in the presence of strong initial magnetic configurations. Consequently, it is a likely contributor to magnetic field generation in environments such as the heliosheath and magnetotail, where strong fields coexist with significant flow shear.

We introduce a novel Semi-supervised Feature-level Trait Manipulation (SFTM) approach to enhance fashion image retrieval. The methodology decomposes garment images into a static background and a dynamic garment component, subsequently extracting deep embeddings for both. Unlike conventional techniques, our framework utilizes a generative adversarial network (GAN) to alter specific garment attributes—such as color or style—within these embedding spaces. By training a metric learning loss on manipulated pairs, the system establishes a robust supervised similarity metric. Crucially, this metric is subsequently refined using unsupervised image data through a self-supervised strategy, resulting in superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines a specific category of ill-posed linear equations within the framework of Banach spaces. Leveraging the theory of regularizing dual gradients, we establish convergence rates for this dual method. Subsequently, we demonstrate that our findings encompass and extend previous outcomes derived from dual gradient approaches tailored to linear inverse problems featuring smoothness constraints. Finally, we validate our mathematical analysis through a numerical experiment focusing on the continuous reconstruction of a function from its Fourier-Laplace data.

We introduce a cost-building strategy for light field depth estimation that integrates structural awareness of occlusions. By constructing the cost map using only intra-structural pixels, the method inherently mitigates issues related to ambiguous occlusions and false disparity matches caused by occlusion gaps and repetitive patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses several leading conventional techniques across various standard light field depth estimation benchmarks.

This paper introduces a new bilinear formulation for the Fokas-Lenells equations. Additionally, we derive explicit expressions for the N-soliton solutions, demonstrating their validity through the use of the new bilinear system.

We present a double field theory framework for non-Riemannian actions that rely exclusively on the generalized Ricci scalar $R$ alongside a finite set of generalized torsion tensors. By examining the generalized torsion components derived from the Ricci scalar dependence, we establish a correspondence between this approach and non-Riemannian theories previously described using the Ricci tensor. Furthermore, we explore a link to non-Riemannian actions formulated in terms of a generalized stress-energy tensor, while also discussing the potential physical interpretations of these generalized torsion forms.

The proliferation of wireless devices in the home environment has created a significant demand for higher bandwidth, driving the adoption of newer IEEE 802.11 standards. To address this, the IEEE has introduced complementary protocols including 802.11k (neighbor discovery), 802.11v (network assisted), and 802.11r (fast handover). This research leverages 802.11k/v protocols to create a client mechanism capable of identifying access points with superior channel loading. Specifically, it involves determining the current channel load of available APs and enabling roaming toward the optimal connection based on these measurements. The proposed algorithm utilizes 802.11k to gather load data from neighboring APs and employs 802.11v to facilitate client migration to the AP offering the best channel conditions. The study validates the effectiveness of this proposed method through both analytical analysis and simulation.
